#9861. NeoMME: an efficient Multimodal-native and Multilingual Encoder

We introduce NeoMME, a family of 260M and 800M multilingual multimodal encoders. Unlike many generative visual language models, NeoMME does not use a separate pretrained vision tower or a causal language model. A single bidirectional Transformer processes both text tokens and raw image patches, and we train the entire model from scratch with a masked discrete-diffusion objective.

We fine-tuned NeoMME for visual document retrieval using ColPali's page-image approach. NeoMME-Retriever returns dense and late-interaction embeddings in one forward pass. Both model sizes lie on the ViDoRe v3 Pareto frontier for nDCG@10 and model size. At a matched 2048×2048 image input size on an NVIDIA L40S GPU, the 260M model encodes about 51 pages per second, or about twice ColModernVBERT's throughput. Hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization reduce late-interaction index storage from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page (255× smaller) while retaining more than 95% of baseline nDCG@10.

NeoMME is available in Hugging Face Transformers. We release all model checkpoints under the Apache 2.0 license.

Many recent visual document retrievers are adapted from pretrained generative visual language models. A separately pretrained vision encoder produces visual features, which a projector maps into the language model's input space. A causal decoder then processes the combined image and text representations. Retrieval, classification, and token labeling do not generate text autoregressively, so they do not require a causal decoder or the parameter and compute overhead of this architecture.

ModernBERT brought efficient architecture and training improvements to bidirectional encoders. For visual document retrieval, ModernVBERT applied a bidirectional ModernBERT-style text encoder while retaining a separate pretrained SigLIP2 vision tower. We wanted to push this even further by designing and training a multimodal encoder without having to carry over the parameter and compute overhead of a VLM.

NeoMME (pronounced "nee-oh-me", IPA /ˈniː.oʊ.mi/) is a multilingual, multimodal foundation encoder that generates vector representations for input text and/or images using a single Transformer encoder. It is not based on an existing pretrained vision tower, text encoder, or text decoder.

Images and text use the same computational path, so NeoMME can more easily support pretraining, fine-tuning, parallelization, and serving across both modalities.

NeoMME comes in two sizes, 260M and 800M. Both variants share the same architecture:

We pretrain NeoMME from scratch as a discrete masked-diffusion text denoiser. For each text-only example, we sample a corruption rate uniformly between 0 and 1. Each eligible text token is then independently masked at that rate.

Multimodal examples use corruption rates between 0.3 and 1. The image patches remain visible while NeoMME reconstructs masked text. With light masking, the model can often recover a missing word from the surrounding text alone. For example, "cat" is a plausible completion of "The [MASK] sat on the mat," even without an image. But high masking forces the model to learn image-grounded descriptions with little to no signal from the non-masked input text tokens.

Pretraining mixes multilingual text, code, mathematics, natural images, and document images. Each model processes about 524 billion packed input tokens, including 290 billion tokens from text-only examples. This text budget is relatively small compared with ModernBERT's 2 trillion training token budget. Hence, we chose the NorMuon optimizer to improve data efficiency during training.

To get a meaningful downstream evaluation of the backbone, we fine-tune NeoMME for visual document retrieval using the page-image methodology introduced by ColPali. While traditional text-based retrieval consists of retrieving text chunks, NeoMME-Retriever ranks document page screenshots and bypasses all the preprocessing OCR steps necessary to extract text from PDFs. Treating the pages as images preserves layout, charts, tables, font type and size, and other visual clues that cannot be captured even by a perfect OCR model.

NeoMME-Retriever reuses the NeoMME backbone but adds two jointly trained heads on top of it for retrieval:

Omar Khattab, who introduced late-interaction in ColBERT, explains why the term is more precise than "multi-vector." It describes the granularity and learnability of the scoring function, not simply the number of stored vectors.

To learn more about late-interaction, we recommend reading this crash course by Amélie Chatelain.

One NeoMME-Retriever forward pass returns both representations, which gives you flexibility no matter your use case and infrastructure. We recommend using late-interaction embeddings in general since they are more powerful and can be used easily with open-source libraries like NextPlaid. However, if you have a very large corpora, you can run a single forward pass with NeoMME-Retriever to get the dense embedding, retrieve a small number of documents through an ANN index, and then use late-interaction to rerank the retrieved candidates.

We report nDCG@10 on ViDoRe v3. NeoMME-Retriever-260M reaches 0.523, the highest score among evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters. It is within 0.002 nDCG@10 of ColQwen2.5 while using about 14× fewer parameters. NeoMME-Retriever-800M reaches 0.556, within 0.009 nDCG@10 of the similarly sized Vultron Retriever Flash (0.8B). Both NeoMME-Retriever models lie on the model-size Pareto frontier.

ViDoRe v1 and v2 use nDCG@5. On both benchmarks, NeoMME-Retriever-260M outperforms ColModernVBERT and the twice-larger ColSmol-500M. NeoMME-Retriever-800M outperforms ColPali v1.3 while using 3.6 times fewer parameters.

† Scores from MTEB. ‡ Results from our own evaluations.

Late-interaction storage scales linearly with the number of vectors in the output embedding. Higher-resolution images contain more patches, so they produce larger embeddings. For example, a 2048×2048 square page produces embeddings containing 4,200 vectors with NeoMME-Retriever, or about 2.1 MB in float32. Across the ViDoRe v3 benchmark, the measured average is about 1.5 MB per document.

To reduce the storage footprint of the late-interaction index, we combine two complementary compression methods:

We tested this setup on ViDoRe v3. With a pooling factor 10 and int8 queries and documents, storage decreased from about 1.5 MB to 39 kB per page, a 39× reduction, while keeping more than 99% of the baseline nDCG@10. A more aggressive configuration uses pooling factor 8, int8 queries, and binary documents. That version uses 6 kB per page (255× smaller) and keeps more than 95% of the original retrieval quality.

Users can pick a compression setting from that frontier based on storage budget and required retrieval quality.

Before you can search a corpus, a retriever model must turn your documents into embeddings, which will be stored in a vector store like Qdrant, Weaviate, or Milvus. Faster encoding makes building and adding new documents to the index faster, thus reducing the GPU uptime and compute cost required.

So we measured image encoding speeds for NeoMME-Retriever against other multimodal document retrievers. We used preprocessed image tensors and calibrated the batch size separately for each model and image size. At a matched 2048×2048 input size on one NVIDIA L40S, NeoMME-Retriever-260M encodes about 51 pages per second, nearly twice ColModernVBERT's 26 pages per second. Both 260M and 800M NeoMME-Retriever models are also faster than the other models we compared on smaller input images.

NeoMME-Retriever (260M and 800M) returns dense and multi-vector embeddings together. The example below scores two text queries against two document-page images with MeanMaxSim late interaction and dense cosine similarity.

We provide separate dense and late-interaction checkpoints for fine-tuning with Sentence Transformers v6. Following the same pattern as text encoders such as ModernBERT, Sentence Transformers loads the backbone through NeoMMEModel rather than the dual-head NeoMMEForRetrieval class. Sentence Transformers currently supports one retrieval head per model, so each checkpoint lets you fine-tune the dense or late-interaction head independently. To train both heads together, use NeoMMEForRetrieval with a custom Trainer.

Visual document retrieval can be used as the first stage of a visual retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system. Unlike text RAG, which retrieves extracted text chunks, visual RAG retrieves the original page images and sends them to a visual language model. The model can then use tables, plots, diagrams, and page layout that text extraction may flatten or omit. Here is how visual RAG works:

You can test visual RAG directly with NeoMME-Retriever in our HF Space: 🤗 tonywu71/neomme-retriever-demo.

NeoMME replaces separate pretrained image and text encoders with one long-context bidirectional Transformer. We train it from scratch to process both multilingual text tokens and raw 32×32 image patches.

NeoMME-Retriever is a fine-tuned version of NeoMME for visual document retrieval. One forward pass produces both dense and late-interaction representations. The 260M model outperforms all evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters and, at a matched 2048×2048 input size, encodes pages at about 2× ColModernVBERT's throughput. To reduce the large storage footprint of late-interaction embeddings for high-resolution documents, we experimented with hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization and managed to reduce the late-interaction embeddings from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page, a 255× compression, while retaining more than 95% of the baseline nDCG@10.

We release all NeoMME model checkpoints and a day-zero Hugging Face Transformers implementation to allow practitioners to build efficient multimodal and multilingual representation models on top of our work.

NeoMME began as a side quest between two good friends. We worked with limited time and compute, and we decided to share the results so the community can build on them. We thank H Company for supporting the work and providing the compute used to train NeoMME.

#9860. Enabling the parallel frontend on nightly

TL;DR: We are enabling the parallel frontend of the Rust compiler on nightly by default, to find remaining issues in preparation for its stabilization.

The Rust compiler has been using multiple threads to compile code in its "backend" part (using LLVM) for a long time. However, its "frontend" part (which includes type checking and borrow checking) has been executing sequentially, on a single thread, which of course limits the performance of the compiler. If you are interested in a more in-depth explanation of parallelism in the Rust compiler, see this previous post.

The compiler frontend actually had support for running in parallel for a long time, but it was not enabled by default due to various issues. Three years ago, we made it possible to opt into the parallel frontend on the nightly channel, with the plan to stabilize it in 2024. Clearly, we did not achieve that goal, but work on the parallel frontend was still slowly progressing in the meantime.

Last year, Vadim Petrochenkov, together with several other contributors, started a coordinated effort to finally get the parallel frontend over the finish line. Since then, many long-standing issues were fixed, and its performance was improved. Now we are at a point where we would like to make it widely available. But before that, we want to find out if people encounter issues with it in the wild, which is why we are enabling it by default only on the nightly channel. Once we will be confident enough that it is working well, we want to stabilize it.

The parallel frontend has been enabled on the nightly channel by default since nightly-2026-11-14.

The primary benefit of enabling the parallel frontend is, of course, faster compilation of Rust programs.

We benchmarked the parallel frontend in our benchmark suite, which measures the duration to compile the leaf crate in a crate graph. As usual, the results were varied. In some benchmarks, the parallel frontend barely helped. In others, for example when performing a cargo check of the nalgebra, cargo or diesel crates, the compilation was almost three times faster, using 8 threads.

In the table below, you can find the aggregated wall-time mean change for the real-world benchmarks in our suite, when building a single crate from scratch across several configurations, compared to the same build using a sequential frontend.

It is clear that the parallelization is not perfect, and we definitely plan to invest more effort into improving its performance. Nevertheless, with 8 threads, it can make the end-to-end compilation time of cargo check ~2x faster for several crates that we tested, which is still quite an improvement.

The performance benefits for incremental rebuilds are much more modest, and also very hard to compare, because the performance of rebuilds depends on what was changed and how were the codegen units laid out. In our benchmark suite, we saw a mean improvement of 3-5% for incremental rebuilds. But we currently do not have great benchmarks for this use-case, so your results might vary.

We can also zoom in on an individual crate. Here is a chart of how the wall-time scales when compiling the nalgebra 0.33 crate, for a full non-incremental build (full), full incremental build (incr-full) and an incremental rebuild (incr-patched) across several build configurations:

What is interesting to note is that enabling the parallel frontend can actually also make the backend faster, for reasons explained here.

It is important to note that all benchmark results presented above measured only the compilation of a single crate. When compiling a whole crate graph, your CPU cores might already be saturated because of backend (LLVM) parallelism or by Cargo compiling multiple crates in parallel. So the final performance effect will vary heavily based on the workload that you are running, and on the number of cores that you have available.

We also benchmarked cargo check end-to-end (checking the whole crate graph) on the cargo crate itself on a machine with 8 CPU cores. With 8 threads, it resulted in a ~15% end-to-end improvement:

As can be seen from the results above, when the CPU cores are already saturated with parallel crate compilation and LLVM, the positive effect of the parallel frontend is reduced.

At the start, the nightly toolchain will default to the parallel frontend using only 2 threads. This is a conservative choice that should still allow us to find potential issues while not increasing memory usage a lot at the same time.

If you want to test out the performance with different thread counts, you can override the number of threads used for the frontend using the --jobs-frontend compiler flag. It can be specified either in the RUSTFLAGS environment variable, or you can put it into a .cargo/config.toml file:

Currently, the performance of the parallel frontend will likely not scale very well above ~8 threads, but you can try it on your workload to test what happens. Note that using higher thread counts will likely lead to higher memory usage of the compiler, and in extreme cases it might cause you to run out of memory.

Due to the used parallelism, the produced order of diagnostics might not be deterministic when using the parallel frontend.

In some situations, the generated binary might also not be reproducible, though we currently consider these cases bugs, and we would like to identify them and fix them.

There are currently some known issues related to the reproducibility of the Rust compiler when using the parallel frontend, which are being worked on.

To reiterate: this is only being enabled on nightly for now. If you are using the stable toolchain, you will still be using the sequential frontend by default.

If you want to disable the parallel frontend on the nightly channel, pass -Zunstable-options --jobs-frontend=1 to rustc, either via the RUSTFLAGS environment variable, or with the .cargo/config.toml configuration file:

If you have to do this for some reason, please do tell us why on GitHub or on Zulip. We would especially like to know about any compiler crashes that you encounter, or the produced binaries not being reproducible when the parallel frontend is enabled.

Over the next few months, we will be monitoring GitHub and Zulip for any reported issues about the parallel frontend. Once we have enough confidence that it is working well, and there are no major issues, we would like to move forward and finally stabilize it.

We would also like to improve its performance, and make more things parallel. So far, a lot of the work on the parallel frontend has been focused on making it work correctly, rather than tuning its performance down to the last percent. We thus expect that we might still be able to make further performance improvements to it.

We would also like to make more parts of the frontend actually parallel, as some parts are currently still sequential even if parallelism is enabled. There is some ongoing work on this. Last year, we had a Google Summer of Code project focused on enabling parallel macro expansion and name resolution, and there is also an open pull request for parallelizing the lowering of the Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) to the High-Level Intermediate Representation (HIR). More work remains to be done on this front.

#9859. PostgreSQL patches 52 security holes, sends version 14 into retirement

Some fixes need more than installation, while the next major release is due November 19

PostgreSQL developers have patched 52 security vulnerabilities and more than 140 bugs in updates spanning versions 14 to 18, alongside a second release candidate for version 19.

The batch includes PostgreSQL 14.25, the final release for the now-unsupported version 14. Users are advised to move to a newer major version.

Some fixes also require follow-up work, including rebuilding affected indexes or taking a fresh full backup. Administrators should check the release's post-update instructions.

Alastair Turner, community technologist at open source consultancy Percona, said the high-severity code execution flaws should be taken seriously, although exploiting them requires database access.

"This isn't something just a brute-force scan of the right port is going to find," he said. "They can make compromises through SQL injection or credential theft a lot worse, but don't create the opportunity for remote, anonymous code execution."

Among the fixes is CVE-2026-6460, a type confusion flaw that could let a database user with permission to create objects execute arbitrary code. It carries a CVSS severity score of 8.8 out of 10.

Turner attributed the growing number of security discoveries partly to AI-assisted scanning and partly to increased scrutiny as PostgreSQL gains ground in enterprise computing.

"It is a record number of CVEs fixed in a quarterly release, and I don't think we've seen the end of that trend. Looking down the list of where these CVEs came from, we see Anthropic and OpenAI open source scanners, so it is clear AI or brute force is playing a role," he said.

Turner said the fixes spanned multiple parts of the software. There "isn't one piece of code that was broken" but rather "a wide base that got patched."

"It's also worth noting that this is the third quarterly release in a row which sets a new record for the number of CVEs patched," he added.

PostgreSQL 14 users now face a major-version upgrade or running without further security and bug fixes. Their destination may depend on internal upgrade policies. Organizations that require the previous major release, known as N-1, would currently target PostgreSQL 17, Turner noted. Version 18 remains the latest generally available release until 19 arrives.

PostgreSQL 19 is scheduled for general availability on Thursday, November 19, barring further problems. It is set to include a new REPACK command, whose CONCURRENTLY option allows reads and writes to continue while disk space is reclaimed. VACUUM FULL requires an exclusive table lock, blocking reads and writes while it runs. ®

#9857. Rebuilding AUTOMATIC1111 with Gradio Workflow

In our last post, we built five small gr.Workflow graphs and hinted at what it would take to build something as complex as AUTOMATIC1111's stable-diffusion-webui. In this post we walk you through Workflow1111, where we have rebuilt most of AUTOMATIC1111's feature set as a single workflow canvas.

Workflow1111 is a graph of eleven media pipelines built using seventy-three nodes. It brings together SOTA models for text-to-image, hi-resolution fix, image-to-image, prompt-matrix grids, VLM interrogate, detection-to-inpaint masks, ControlNet-style annotators, background removal, PNG Info storing, and image-to-video.

You can run any of these pipelines by signing in with your Hugging Face account or providing an access token. Once you sign in, the model calls use your own quota.

👉 Try Workflow1111, or duplicate the Space and start rewiring it for your own use case.

All the media pipelines are built from the same four operator kinds covered in our last post and the official guide. Each node on the canvas wraps one operator, and the operator's inputs and outputs become the ports you connect edges to. As a quick reference on our four operator kinds: fn is a Python function, model is a model called through InferenceClient, space is another Gradio Space, and dataset is a row from a Hub dataset.

Let's go through the pipelines one by one.

This is the core pipeline. It has the controls you'd expect from A1111's txt2img tab: negative prompt, steps, CFG, seed, width and height, plus a model_id field for choosing the checkpoint. The prompt goes through a prompt-builder fn node first, which appends the selected style preset and cleans up the text, then into a model node that calls the checkpoint through Inference Providers. A post-process fn node writes the generation parameters into the PNG's metadata on the way out, which is what the PNG Info pipeline reads back later.

In Automatic1111, hi-resolution fix first upscales the txt2img output and then runs a second denoising pass. Here it's a two-node detour instead. The text-to-image result goes into a FLUX.1-Kontext model node with a refine instruction ("enhance fine detail and micro-texture, keep the composition identical") and comes back sharper and larger.

That same Kontext node doubles as the image-to-image tab. Upload an image, describe the change you want, and it returns the edited image.

Start with a rough prompt like "A lighthouse in a storm." This pipeline sends it to a Qwen3-4B model node, and a small fn node turns the reply into a clean list of tags, capped at forty: "stormy sea, wet rocks, dramatic composition, low angle shot, volumetric lighting, ominous tone." You can connect any diffusion model node to this output to render the image.

There's no custom node involved, unlike in ComfyUI. In a Gradio workflow the LLM and the diffusion model are both ordinary model operators on the same canvas.

This is like AUTOMATIC1111's Interrogate button, with a VLM doing the interrogating instead of CLIP. Qwen2.5-VL looks at a night-market photo and writes a prompt that could have produced it. A ViT classifier node reads the same image and returns labels: restaurant 51.9%, tobacco shop 15.6%, toyshop 9.1%.

Both nodes use the same image input, so gr.Workflow runs them in parallel and you get both answers in roughly the time it takes to run one.

AUTOMATIC1111 makes you paint an inpaint mask by hand. This pipeline generates one from a detector instead. DETR finds six objects in a street photo (three people, a dog, a bicycle, and a car), and from there the workflow splits into two branches: one draws the detected boxes on the original image, the other turns them into a mask you can feed into an inpaint pipeline downstream.

The drawing and the mask creation both happen locally with Pillow and NumPy. Only the detection call leaves the machine.

This is like AUTOMATIC1111's prompt matrix. A base prompt, "a lone oak tree," gets combined with four suffixes (at sunrise, in a thunderstorm, under the Milky Way, in autumn fog) by a fn node, and each variant goes to its own text-to-image node. A final node stitches the four results into one contact sheet.

gr.Workflow has no loop operator, so the four text-to-image nodes sit side by side on the canvas. Since they're at the same dependency depth they run in parallel, and all four images start generating at once.

This is like the Extras tab in Automatic1111. There are two upscaler nodes, and they take different routes. The first is a local Lanczos resample in an fn node, which needs no network call and finishes as fast as Pillow can resize. The second is AuraSR ×4, and it's the first space node on the canvas: it calls a Space on the Hub and treats the result like any other node output.

Background removal works the same way. BRIA RMBG-2.0 is another space node, so the whole model lives in its own Space and this canvas just calls it in.

Canny, line art, sketch, luma-depth, and posterize are the preprocessors you'd normally get from the ControlNet extension in Automatic1111. Here, each one is a fn node written in plain NumPy, with no model behind it. On a pre-loaded example photo of a building facade, each annotator takes about half a second on CPU.

There are 36 operator nodes in the app, 32 are fn nodes, and 22 of those run entirely in-process without a network call. Roughly two-thirds of the canvas keeps working if you lose your connection. Since these are regular Python functions, you can also test them directly, with no canvas, server, or GPU involved.

AUTOMATIC1111 stores generation details in the PNG's parameters text chunk, and the PNG Info tab reads them back. Workflow1111 does the same. The post-process node on the text-to-image pipeline writes the metadata, and this pipeline reads it back out, including the prompt, negative prompt, steps, CFG, seed, image size, and model.

The image node that PNG Info reads from also feeds a Wan 2.2 I2V A14B node, which animates it; in the demo example a sleeping fox wakes up and starts moving. There's no second upload box because one reference node can feed as many downstream pipelines as you need, so a single upload gets its metadata read and gets animated on the same canvas.

So far every model call has gone to someone else's hardware, through Inference Providers or a Space. That's why you can build and run something like Workflow1111 without a GPU of your own.

A fn node is just Python, though, so it can equally load a model locally and run it on your own GPU. FastVideo/fastvideo-fasth3-preview is a gr.Workflow app that does exactly that. It runs FastH3, a four-step distillation of MiniMax-H3, and generates video with a soundtrack on ZeroGPU.

The whole app comes down to one bound function:

ZeroGPU gives the function a GPU when it needs one, then releases it when the call is done. gr.Workflow doesn't need to know about any of that. It just calls the fn node.

This isn't specific to Spaces either. Point bind= to a function that loads a local checkpoint, run .launch() on your own machine, and the Workflow1111 canvas can drive your own GPU.

Every output node on the canvas becomes a REST endpoint, with no routes written by hand. Workflow1111 exposes nine of them: /image, /edited_image, /generated_prompt, /recovered_prompt, /detected_objects, /x_y_grid, /upscaled_local, /annotator_map, and /png_info.

The same endpoints are also MCP tools. Launch with mcp_server=True (guide) and every output node shows up as a tool an AI assistant can call. Point Claude Code, Cursor, or any MCP client at the server URL:

Now an agent can generate an image, read a prompt back out, or run detection as steps in a larger task, with no glue code. Each caller sends their own token in the X-HF-Token header, so the Space holds none of its own.

AUTOMATIC1111 gave us the feature list, but the tool Gradio Workflow really gets compared to is ComfyUI, since both are node graphs. For a lot of what people want to build and ship, gr.Workflow covers the same ground.

The result is a multi-model pipeline that people can open in a browser, sign into, use right away, and call from code.

Workflow1111 has 73 nodes, but it started with just this:

bind= turns your functions into nodes, edges= connects them, and .launch() opens the canvas in your browser so you can keep editing there. When it's ready, gradio deploy puts the whole thing on a Space. The gr.Workflow guide has the full details, including the JSON schema and every operator type.

If you'd rather start from something that already works, open Workflow1111, hit Duplicate, and pick one of the eleven pipelines to change: delete nodes, swap models, rewire the flow. If you'd rather start smaller, the previous post has five workflows you can get running in about a minute each.

Whatever you build, post it on X and tag @gradio. We'd be happy to amplify your workflows.

4-step MiniMax-H3 — video with a matching soundtrack

Automatic1111-style studio on one gr.Workflow canvas

Really impressive breakdown the part that stands out most is how the graph structure gives you free parallelism (the prompt-matrix and interrogate examples) without any extra orchestration code. The mix of fn, model, and space node types on one canvas also makes the ComfyUI comparison land well: you get custom-node flexibility from plain Python, but zero-code REST/MCP endpoints for free. Curious how complex a canvas can get before performance or maintainability becomes a concern has anyone pushed past 73 nodes

Analisis yang sangat mengesankan, bagian yang paling menonjol adalah bagaimana struktur graf memberikan paralelisme gratis (contoh prompt-matrix dan interrogate) tanpa kode orkestrasi tambahan. Perpaduan tipe node fn, model, dan space pada satu kanvas juga membuat perbandingan dengan ComfyUI tepat: Anda mendapatkan fleksibilitas node kustom dari Python biasa, tetapi endpoint REST/MCP tanpa kode secara gratis. Saya penasaran seberapa kompleks sebuah kanvas dapat dibuat sebelum kinerja atau pemeliharaan menjadi masalah, apakah ada yang pernah melampaui 73 node?

#9856. MPs ask what the break clause was for as Palantir wins two more years in the NHS

Ministers promise fresh procurement, but critics warn extension gives US supplier more time to dig in

Lawmakers and campaign groups have slammed the UK government's decision to extend Palantir's controversial NHS contract by two years.

Health minister James Frith told MPs on Monday that the current contract would continue until March 2029 as the government procures a new version of the Federated Data Platform (FDP). The existing Palantir-led deal, awarded in 2023, has a maximum value of £330 million and includes other suppliers.

Frith said the new procurement would focus on interoperability, resilience, and trusted common standards in a "new FDP iteration" which would "welcome international and UK capability alike – whether that is UK small and medium-sized enterprises that want a crack at NHS contracts, sovereign AI-backed capability in the UK or any international provider worth merit."

Palantir's cornerstone NHS contract win attracted criticism for lack of transparency. The US supplier had already won £60 million in NHS contracts without competition during and following the pandemic. Use cases from this period were carried over to the FDP. Critics have also challenged the evidence used to promote the FDP's claimed benefits.

Dame Chi Onwurah, chair of the Commons Science and Technology Committee, said she was "extremely disappointed" by the decision. She challenged the government's reliance on continuity of care to justify keeping the contract, given its existing transition provisions. She said Palantir made it clear it would use the next two years to "embed itself even more deeply in our public services."

"If a break clause cannot be exercised because of continuity of care, it is not a break clause; it is a lock-in. The Minister assured me that there were already contractual requirements that smooth continuity of care should continue. Were those assurances made in error?" she asked Frith.

Frith confirmed that the contracts included exit and transition provisions and that migration was "possible in principle."

"However, given the requirement for a new iteration, given performance and the benefits already in play, and given the opportunity to add new capability, including maternity services, to a next generation of FDP, an 18 to 24-month period for commission and procurement is a reasonable assessment," he said.

Technology and government priorities had moved on since the original FDP procurement in 2023, he told MPs. "We will begin a new procurement process along different lines from the current contract," he said.

The formal process is set to start during the second half of next year and take around 18 months.

"Interoperability, resilience, and trusted common standards can and must be baked into the next generation of FDP. We will also start work, alongside the new procurement, with different providers on developing new capabilities and expertise starting with systems used in maternity care. Innovative providers will be invited to help address the data and digital fragmentation in this important area of care, and test how health priorities can create routes to build UK AI capability," Frith said.

Former Labour deputy leader Tom Watson, now Palantir's UK senior vice president, welcomed the extension.

"This is good news for patients and for the NHS. And it is the right decision to press forward with a programme that, in the words of Ministers, 'is significantly exceeding its benefits forecast and has exceeded every target' since it launched in 2024," he said.

"We will now redouble our efforts over the next two years to continue and accelerate that support. As a result of the announcement, we will also deepen our investment in the UK. The FDP is the right vehicle to deliver the change needed in the NHS, and over the next two years Palantir will do everything in its power to drive that change as far as possible, as fast as possible."

Nonprofit tech transparency group Foxglove has challenged NHS contracts awarded to Palantir without competition since the pandemic, when the company initially offered its services for £1.

Responding to the extension, Foxglove co-executive director Rosa Curling said:  "Palantir and its chief lobbyist Lord Tom Watson clearly think the contract extension is in the bag and appear to be already planning to turn that into another extension in two years, or a new procurement that heavily favors Palantir as we saw in 2023.

"The government must provide urgent clarity on whether they plan to help Watson embed Palantir in the NHS for the long term – or will kick this Trump-backing spy tech company out of the health service once and for all." ®

Good, it's automatically monitoring the chemicals. Bad, it doesn't actually do anything about it except send an email.

For life and safety things, alerts are often closed-loop. That is, the system actually checks the alarm went off.

This can lead to some really interesting things - your car plays various beeps and chimes to indicate various status things. But did you know there is a microphone in the car listening to make sure those chimes actually play? Or if you have one of the fancy cars with LCD screens, every time it pops up an idiot light, the screen is actually read back by the controller to verify that the indication is actually displayed. The same goes for medical equipment - all those alarms and beeps are monitored and the equipment is making sure it's playing those sounds.

Critical alarms should have a backup system and a test system. It's why industrial control systems have lamp tests where you can verify the lamp is functional and not burned out. But also if a critical alert happens, it has a bunch of ways to alert you something has gone wrong. Even just having a loud klaxon would often get the attention of someone who could possibly be affected or at least people asking why there's a loud annoying sound being played.

#9854. How to Bypass Rust's Orphan Rule

Write Rust for long enough, and you are bound to run into error[E0117].Take a simple, everyday scenario. You pull in a serialization library that defines a ToJson trait, along with a third-party type library like uuid. You want to turn a uuid::Uuid into JSON, so you naturally write:impl ToJson for uuid::Uuid { fn to_json(&self) -> String { format!("\"{}\"", self) } }And the compiler immediately stops you:error[E0117]: only traits defined in the current crate can be implemented for types defined outside of the crateThis is Rust's well-known Orphan Rule. Once people hit this wall, they usually either complain that the compiler is too rigid or dutifully wrap the type in a NewType. But if you look closely at how the Orphan Rule actually works, it is not a dead end. By design, it leaves a pretty wide door open.What Is the Orphan Rule Actually Protecting Against?Setting the jargon aside, the logic behind the Orphan Rule is simple: if you want a type to implement a trait, at least one of those two things (the type or the trait) must belong to your own crate. In plain English, you don't get to make rules for someone else's types.Suppose crate A implements ToJson for uuid::Uuid and outputs a hyphenated UUID string, while crate B also implements ToJson for uuid::Uuid and outputs 32 raw hex characters without hyphens. If a project depends on both A and B, the compiler has a problem when it sees uuid.to_json(): which implementation should it pick?To prevent this kind of global conflict, Rust enforces coherence, and the Orphan Rule is how it gets enforced. There is nothing wrong with the rule itself. It keeps the Rust ecosystem from turning into a mess as dependency trees grow. The catch is that real-world projects constantly run into a very common need: making a third-party type implement a trait from another third-party crate. Neither the type nor the trait is yours, yet gluing libraries together like this happens all the time. So what can you do?Why the Two Usual Workarounds Fall ShortRight now, the Rust ecosystem mostly relies on two workarounds. Both appear to solve the problem on the surface, but because neither addresses the root cause, they get awkward fast.1. Building it into the libraryMany foundational crates take this route: since users can't write the impl themselves, the crate provides it internally. Because ToJson is defined inside the crate, implementing it for any external type satisfies the Orphan Rule. Open up the Cargo.toml of one of these crates, and you will see a long list of feature flags: with-uuid, with-chrono, with-time, with-jiff, with-url, with-rust-decimal, and so on.It looks helpful at first, but it tries to enumerate an open, constantly changing ecosystem inside a single crate. That approach has clear limits, and the downsides show up quickly:You can never support everything. Today the community favors chrono, tomorrow people switch to jiff, and next week your team builds its own internal Money type. If the library doesn't have built-in support, you are stuck waiting for a release or opening a PR yourself.Version lock-in. When a third-party type crate bumps its major version, your whole dependency tree gets stuck until the trait crate publishes a matching update.Hardcoded behavior. Maybe the library serializes DateTime as an ISO-8601 string by default, while your API spec requires an integer timestamp in milliseconds. Because the implementation lives inside the library, you have no way to change it.2. Wrap it in a NewType yourselfWhen the library doesn't have built-in support, or its default behavior doesn't fit your needs, you fall back to the familiar NewType pattern:pub struct MyUuid(pub uuid::Uuid); impl ToJson for MyUuid { fn to_json(&self) -> String { format!("\"{}\"", self.0) } }Wrapping one or two types is fine. The trouble starts when a moderately complex domain model mixes Uuid, Url, DateTime, HashMap, and custom domain types all at once. Once you wrap everything into MyUuid, MyUrl, and MyDateTime, your business logic gets littered with .0, and you spend your time constantly wrapping and unwrapping values. It gets old very quickly.NewType is a genuinely useful pattern in Rust for expressing domain meaning, hiding internals, or enforcing invariants. The problem is that when you only use it to appease the Orphan Rule on types that didn't need a wrapper in the first place, your code bloats quickly.So is there a way to let users decide how third-party types implement a trait, without wrapping everything in NewTypes?Adding a Generic Slot to the TraitLet's go back to the rule: either the type or the trait must belong to the current crate.Many developers assume the compiler only looks at Trait and Type in impl Trait for Type. In fact, under Rust's Orphan Rule (RFC 2451), the trait's own generic type parameters are also part of the check.Put simply, in impl Trait

for Type, as long as a local type appears in the trait's generic parameters, and there are no uncovered type parameters before it, the compiler knows this implementation belongs exclusively to the current crate. No other crate can conflict with it, so the compiler lets it through.Take this example:impl ToJson for uuid::Uuid { // ... }ToJson is a foreign trait, and Uuid is a foreign type, but MyApp is defined in the current crate. Because it sits in the trait's generic parameter position, this impl satisfies the Orphan Rule.Following this idea, a library author only needs to take one extra step when designing a trait: leave a generic parameter on the trait as an extension point for users.For example:pub trait ToJson { fn to_json(&self) -> String; }Notice that Ctx = () has a default type. When the library implements ToJson for basic types like i32 and String, it makes those implementations generic over any Ctx:impl ToJson for i32 { fn to_json(&self) -> String { self.to_string() } } impl ToJson for String { fn to_json(&self) -> String { format!("\"{}\"", self) } }This way, regular users never even notice Ctx exists. Everything works the exact same way as before, with () as the default context.When you do need to plug in third-party types, you just define an empty marker struct in your own crate:pub struct MyApp;Then you can write implementations for any third-party type you want:impl ToJson for uuid::Uuid { fn to_json(&self) -> String { format!("\"{}\"", self) } } impl ToJson for chrono::DateTime { fn to_json(&self) -> String { self.timestamp_millis().to_string() } }The compiler looks at this and sees: ToJson is foreign, Uuid and DateTime are foreign, but MyApp is local to your crate. No other crate can write a conflicting implementation using your MyApp, so global coherence is completely safe. It compiles right away.You can think of this conversion setup as a web of relationships, with your local MyApp type as its root. A handy way to picture it is a bunch of grapes, where MyApp is the stem. Once you grab that stem, it doesn't matter how many third-party types hang off it (Uuid, Url, DateTime, HashMap, and so on). You lift the whole bunch at once, and the compiler accepts all of them as local implementations.Better yet, you can define more than one stem in the same project. For instance, your HTTP API layer can use ApiCtx to format timestamps as strings, while an internal RPC layer uses RpcCtx to format them as integer timestamps. Both sets of rules live under separate contexts, completely isolated at compile time, with zero conflict.One detail to watch out for: the local type has to be a real, newly defined type. Creating a type alias for a foreign type will not work.The Position of the Local Type MattersAt this point, you might think that dropping a local type MyApp anywhere into a trait's generic list solves the Orphan Rule for good. Most of the time, it does. But if your trait has more than one generic parameter, or if you want to write a generic impl, there is an ordering restriction that is easy to trip over.When the compiler runs its Orphan Rule check, it scans the types in a fixed order: first the Self type, then the trait's 1st generic parameter, then the 2nd, and so on. The rule comes down to one sentence: no bare generic type parameter T may appear before the first local type.Code makes this clearest. Suppose an external crate defines ForeignTrait and ForeignType, and you define MyApp locally:// ✅ Allowed: scans ForeignType, then hits local MyApp first; the trailing T is unrestricted impl ForeignTrait for ForeignType {} // ❌ Error: hits a bare T before seeing MyApp impl ForeignTrait for ForeignType {} // ❌ Error: hits a bare T right away in Self, before MyApp gets a chance impl ForeignTrait for T {}The only word to pay attention to here is "bare". In Rust terminology, this is called an uncovered type parameter. A plain T is uncovered. If it is wrapped inside a non-fundamental concrete type like Vec (built-in fundamental types like &T and Box do not count), it is no longer uncovered, so it will not block a local MyApp that comes after it:// ✅ Allowed: T is covered by Vec, so it is not an uncovered type parameter impl ForeignTrait, MyApp> for ForeignType {}From a library author's perspective, this means it is not enough to just add a generic slot; you also need to put it in the right place. If your trait has multiple generic parameters and there is no strong reason otherwise, put the context Ctx in the first type parameter position. That way, downstream users writing generic implementations can avoid most of the surprising Orphan Rule errors.A Truly Standalone models CrateOnce this mechanism clicks, you will see that it also solves a stubborn architectural headache in larger Rust codebases.As a project grows, it usually gets split into a Cargo workspace: maybe an API gateway crate, a few business service crates, and a background worker crate. These modules often share the same data structures, so the natural move is to pull those structs out into a standalone models crate.Traditionally, doing this in Rust is painful. Suppose models defines a Product struct with Uuid, Url, and DateTime fields. If your serialization library or ORM expects those field types to already implement its traits inside models, you are left with two bad options:Wrap everything in NewTypes inside models, and pull in the serialization library, database driver, and other heavy dependencies along with them. A crate that was supposed to hold plain data structures ends up with the heaviest dependency tree in the workspace.Give up on splitting it out, and dump models and business logic into the same crate. It saves time early on, but dependency boundaries and compile times get harder to manage as the project grows.With the generic Ctx parameter, that knot comes untied. Inside your standalone models crate, you just define your structs with native types:// crate: models pub struct Product { pub id: uuid::Uuid, pub created_at: chrono::DateTime, }Then you write a generic implementation for Product open to any Ctx (or let a derive macro generate it):impl ToJson for Product where uuid::Uuid: ToJson, chrono::DateTime: ToJson { fn to_json(&self) -> String { format!( "{{\"id\":{},\"created_at\":{}}}", ToJson::::to_json(&self.id), ToJson::::to_json(&self.created_at), ) } }Notice the subtle part here: inside the models crate, Uuid and DateTime do not implement ToJson yet, and this code still compiles.That is because models is only declaring a deferred contract: "whoever uses this later, as long as your context Ctx knows how to handle Uuid and DateTime, Product automatically supports ToJson under your context." As a result, models stays completely lightweight, carries no concrete conversion logic, and compiles very fast. The actual conversions are deferred to the downstream service crates, where each service hooks up what it needs using its own local context.For large workspaces, this keeps dependency boundaries clean. Models can evolve on their own, while different services remain free to pick whatever storage format or API representation they need.Real-World Example: How This Works in KovaThe ToJson snippet above is as minimal as it gets. Does this idea still hold up when you bring it into a real, more complex project?When building my own Rust ORM, Kova, I applied this pattern across the entire type system. It is a good concrete example of how this plays out in practice.ORMs are where the Orphan Rule hurts the most. A single table often mixes Uuid, Url, DateTime, HashMap, and custom domain types. Kova's core Encode and Decode traits use the exact generic slot design we just walked through:pub trait Encode<'a, X = ()> { fn encode(self) -> Result>; } pub trait Decode: Sized { fn decode(value: Value<'_>) -> Result; }Because Kova hands the extension point to the user, it only needs built-in support for basic database primitives: integers, floats, booleans, strings, and byte arrays. Its Cargo.toml does not have to maintain a pile of optional dependencies and feature flags for uuid, chrono, jiff, url, and so on.In a real application, the workflow looks just like the earlier example.First, define your table structs with native types in a standalone models crate and add #[derive(Model)]:// crate: models (no database driver or codec code needed) #[derive(Model)] pub struct Product { pub id: Uuid, pub price: Decimal, pub vendor_url: Url, pub created_at: DateTime, }#[derive(Model)] expands into an open contract like impl Model for Product where ..., so models compiles completely on its own without tying itself to any concrete codec implementation.Next, in your downstream service crate, define a local marker struct pub struct AppCodec; and implement zero-copy conversions matching your storage layout:pub struct AppCodec; // Store Uuid as 16 raw bytes, borrowing directly with zero copies impl<'a, 'b: 'a> Encode<'a, AppCodec> for &'b Uuid { fn encode(self) -> Result> { Ok(Value::Blob(Cow::Borrowed(self.as_bytes()))) } } // Store DateTime as an integer millisecond timestamp impl<'a> Encode<'a, AppCodec> for DateTime { fn encode(self) -> Result> { Ok(Value::Int8(self.timestamp_millis())) } }Finally, switch the client's context marker when you need it:// Default client using the () codec let client = Options::from(conn_str).build()?; // Switch to the local AppCodec at zero runtime cost let client = client.codec::();Switching the type carries zero runtime overhead; under the hood, it only swaps a PhantomData marker on Client from () to AppCodec. And while building Kova, another nice benefit showed up: once you have a local type like AppCodec, you can attach much more to it than just encoding and decoding.For example, suppose you have implemented Encode for url::Url in an ORM. If you still can't run LIKE queries on a Url column, or compare a Url column directly against a &str, that type still feels second-class in queries.So Kova puts the same generic extension slot on its SQL capability traits and type compatibility rules, such as CanString, CanMath, and Compatible. Users can add a couple of short declarations under their own AppCodec:// Give Url string capabilities (enabling methods like `like` and `ilike`) impl CanString for Url {} // Allow passing &str directly to a Url column without calling Url::parse() every time impl<'a> Compatible, AppCodec> for Static<&'a str> {}With that in place, third-party types fit right into the ORM's DSL and behave no differently from built-in types:client .update::() .set(Product::vendor_url.set("https://rust-lang.org")) .filter( Product::id.eq(&target_uuid) & Product::vendor_url.ilike("https://%") ) .execute() .await?;Putting this design through a real codebase like Kova confirmed something practical: opening up type conversions and capabilities to a user-defined context does more than just get around the Orphan Rule on paper. Even in a complex framework, it keeps dependency boundaries clean, compile times fast, and day-to-day usage comfortable.Rust's Orphan Rule is not there to make life hard. It exists to prevent global implementation conflicts and stop crates from stepping on each other in the global namespace. Once you stop fighting for a "globally unique" implementation and instead leave a generic slot on the trait to scope uniqueness to a local context, bypassing the Orphan Rule takes no black magic at all. It is just a simple shift in perspective, yet it makes both library design and large workspace boundaries much cleaner.In the next post, I will talk about the problem that immediately follows this design: once your traits and query builders carry a generic context parameter, how do you avoid falling into generic type gymnastics and monomorphization bloat? That brings us to boundary validation and type erasure.

Maybe the library serializes DateTime as an ISO-8601 string by default, while your API spec requires an integer timestamp in milliseconds. Because the implementation lives inside the library, you have no way to change it.2. Wrap it in a NewType yourselfWhen the library doesn't have built-in support, or its default behavior doesn't fit your needs, you fall back to the familiar NewType pattern:pub struct MyUuid(pub uuid::Uuid); impl ToJson for MyUuid { fn to_json(&self) -> String { format!("\"{}\"", self.0) } }Wrapping one or two types is fine. The trouble starts when a moderately complex domain model mixes Uuid, Url, DateTime, HashMap, and custom domain types all at once. Once you wrap everything into MyUuid, MyUrl, and MyDateTime, your business logic gets littered with .0, and you spend your time constantly wrapping and unwrapping values. It gets old very quickly.NewType is a genuinely useful pattern in Rust for expressing domain meaning, hiding internals, or enforcing invariants. The problem is that when you only use it to appease the Orphan Rule on types that didn't need a wrapper in the first place, your code bloats quickly.So is there a way to let users decide how third-party types implement a trait, without wrapping everything in NewTypes?Adding a Generic Slot to the TraitLet's go back to the rule: either the type or the trait must belong to the current crate.Many developers assume the compiler only looks at Trait and Type in impl Trait for Type. In fact, under Rust's Orphan Rule (RFC 2451), the trait's own generic type parameters are also part of the check.Put simply, in impl Trait

for Type, as long as a local type appears in the trait's generic parameters, and there are no uncovered type parameters before it, the compiler knows this implementation belongs exclusively to the current crate. No other crate can conflict with it, so the compiler lets it through.Take this example:impl ToJson for uuid::Uuid { // ... }ToJson is a foreign trait, and Uuid is a foreign type, but MyApp is defined in the current crate. Because it sits in the trait's generic parameter position, this impl satisfies the Orphan Rule.Following this idea, a library author only needs to take one extra step when designing a trait: leave a generic parameter on the trait as an extension point for users.For example:pub trait ToJson { fn to_json(&self) -> String; }Notice that Ctx = () has a default type. When the library implements ToJson for basic types like i32 and String, it makes those implementations generic over any Ctx:impl ToJson for i32 { fn to_json(&self) -> String { self.to_string() } } impl ToJson for String { fn to_json(&self) -> String { format!("\"{}\"", self) } }This way, regular users never even notice Ctx exists. Everything works the exact same way as before, with () as the default context.When you do need to plug in third-party types, you just define an empty marker struct in your own crate:pub struct MyApp;Then you can write implementations for any third-party type you want:impl ToJson for uuid::Uuid { fn to_json(&self) -> String { format!("\"{}\"", self) } } impl ToJson for chrono::DateTime { fn to_json(&self) -> String { self.timestamp_millis().to_string() } }The compiler looks at this and sees: ToJson is foreign, Uuid and DateTime are foreign, but MyApp is local to your crate. No other crate can write a conflicting implementation using your MyApp, so global coherence is completely safe. It compiles right away.You can think of this conversion setup as a web of relationships, with your local MyApp type as its root. A handy way to picture it is a bunch of grapes, where MyApp is the stem. Once you grab that stem, it doesn't matter how many third-party types hang off it (Uuid, Url, DateTime, HashMap, and so on). You lift the whole bunch at once, and the compiler accepts all of them as local implementations.Better yet, you can define more than one stem in the same project. For instance, your HTTP API layer can use ApiCtx to format timestamps as strings, while an internal RPC layer uses RpcCtx to format them as integer timestamps. Both sets of rules live under separate contexts, completely isolated at compile time, with zero conflict.One detail to watch out for: the local type has to be a real, newly defined type. Creating a type alias for a foreign type will not work.The Position of the Local Type MattersAt this point, you might think that dropping a local type MyApp anywhere into a trait's generic list solves the Orphan Rule for good. Most of the time, it does. But if your trait has more than one generic parameter, or if you want to write a generic impl, there is an ordering restriction that is easy to trip over.When the compiler runs its Orphan Rule check, it scans the types in a fixed order: first the Self type, then the trait's 1st generic parameter, then the 2nd, and so on. The rule comes down to one sentence: no bare generic type parameter T may appear before the first local type.Code makes this clearest. Suppose an external crate defines ForeignTrait and ForeignType, and you define MyApp locally:// ✅ Allowed: scans ForeignType, then hits local MyApp first; the trailing T is unrestricted impl ForeignTrait for ForeignType {} // ❌ Error: hits a bare T before seeing MyApp impl ForeignTrait for ForeignType {} // ❌ Error: hits a bare T right away in Self, before MyApp gets a chance impl ForeignTrait for T {}The only word to pay attention to here is "bare". In Rust terminology, this is called an uncovered type parameter. A plain T is uncovered. If it is wrapped inside a non-fundamental concrete type like Vec (built-in fundamental types like &T and Box do not count), it is no longer uncovered, so it will not block a local MyApp that comes after it:// ✅ Allowed: T is covered by Vec, so it is not an uncovered type parameter impl ForeignTrait, MyApp> for ForeignType {}From a library author's perspective, this means it is not enough to just add a generic slot; you also need to put it in the right place. If your trait has multiple generic parameters and there is no strong reason otherwise, put the context Ctx in the first type parameter position. That way, downstream users writing generic implementations can avoid most of the surprising Orphan Rule errors.A Truly Standalone models CrateOnce this mechanism clicks, you will see that it also solves a stubborn architectural headache in larger Rust codebases.As a project grows, it usually gets split into a Cargo workspace: maybe an API gateway crate, a few business service crates, and a background worker crate. These modules often share the same data structures, so the natural move is to pull those structs out into a standalone models crate.Traditionally, doing this in Rust is painful. Suppose models defines a Product struct with Uuid, Url, and DateTime fields. If your serialization library or ORM expects those field types to already implement its traits inside models, you are left with two bad options:Wrap everything in NewTypes inside models, and pull in the serialization library, database driver, and other heavy dependencies along with them. A crate that was supposed to hold plain data structures ends up with the heaviest dependency tree in the workspace.Give up on splitting it out, and dump models and business logic into the same crate. It saves time early on, but dependency boundaries and compile times get harder to manage as the project grows.With the generic Ctx parameter, that knot comes untied. Inside your standalone models crate, you just define your structs with native types:// crate: models pub struct Product { pub id: uuid::Uuid, pub created_at: chrono::DateTime, }Then you write a generic implementation for Product open to any Ctx (or let a derive macro generate it):impl ToJson for Product where uuid::Uuid: ToJson, chrono::DateTime: ToJson { fn to_json(&self) -> String { format!( "{{\"id\":{},\"created_at\":{}}}", ToJson::::to_json(&self.id), ToJson::::to_json(&self.created_at), ) } }Notice the subtle part here: inside the models crate, Uuid and DateTime do not implement ToJson yet, and this code still compiles.That is because models is only declaring a deferred contract: "whoever uses this later, as long as your context Ctx knows how to handle Uuid and DateTime, Product automatically supports ToJson under your context." As a result, models stays completely lightweight, carries no concrete conversion logic, and compiles very fast. The actual conversions are deferred to the downstream service crates, where each service hooks up what it needs using its own local context.For large workspaces, this keeps dependency boundaries clean. Models can evolve on their own, while different services remain free to pick whatever storage format or API representation they need.Real-World Example: How This Works in KovaThe ToJson snippet above is as minimal as it gets. Does this idea still hold up when you bring it into a real, more complex project?When building my own Rust ORM, Kova, I applied this pattern across the entire type system. It is a good concrete example of how this plays out in practice.ORMs are where the Orphan Rule hurts the most. A single table often mixes Uuid, Url, DateTime, HashMap, and custom domain types. Kova's core Encode and Decode traits use the exact generic slot design we just walked through:pub trait Encode<'a, X = ()> { fn encode(self) -> Result>; } pub trait Decode: Sized { fn decode(value: Value<'_>) -> Result; }Because Kova hands the extension point to the user, it only needs built-in support for basic database primitives: integers, floats, booleans, strings, and byte arrays. Its Cargo.toml does not have to maintain a pile of optional dependencies and feature flags for uuid, chrono, jiff, url, and so on.In a real application, the workflow looks just like the earlier example.First, define your table structs with native types in a standalone models crate and add #[derive(Model)]:// crate: models (no database driver or codec code needed) #[derive(Model)] pub struct Product { pub id: Uuid, pub price: Decimal, pub vendor_url: Url, pub created_at: DateTime, }#[derive(Model)] expands into an open contract like impl Model for Product where ..., so models compiles completely on its own without tying itself to any concrete codec implementation.Next, in your downstream service crate, define a local marker struct pub struct AppCodec; and implement zero-copy conversions matching your storage layout:pub struct AppCodec; // Store Uuid as 16 raw bytes, borrowing directly with zero copies impl<'a, 'b: 'a> Encode<'a, AppCodec> for &'b Uuid { fn encode(self) -> Result> { Ok(Value::Blob(Cow::Borrowed(self.as_bytes()))) } } // Store DateTime as an integer millisecond timestamp impl<'a> Encode<'a, AppCodec> for DateTime { fn encode(self) -> Result> { Ok(Value::Int8(self.timestamp_millis())) } }Finally, switch the client's context marker when you need it:// Default client using the () codec let client = Options::from(conn_str).build()?; // Switch to the local AppCodec at zero runtime cost let client = client.codec::();Switching the type carries zero runtime overhead; under the hood, it only swaps a PhantomData marker on Client from () to AppCodec. And while building Kova, another nice benefit showed up: once you have a local type like AppCodec, you can attach much more to it than just encoding and decoding.For example, suppose you have implemented Encode for url::Url in an ORM. If you still can't run LIKE queries on a Url column, or compare a Url column directly against a &str, that type still feels second-class in queries.So Kova puts the same generic extension slot on its SQL capability traits and type compatibility rules, such as CanString, CanMath, and Compatible. Users can add a couple of short declarations under their own AppCodec:// Give Url string capabilities (enabling methods like `like` and `ilike`) impl CanString for Url {} // Allow passing &str directly to a Url column without calling Url::parse() every time impl<'a> Compatible, AppCodec> for Static<&'a str> {}With that in place, third-party types fit right into the ORM's DSL and behave no differently from built-in types:client .update::() .set(Product::vendor_url.set("https://rust-lang.org")) .filter( Product::id.eq(&target_uuid) & Product::vendor_url.ilike("https://%") ) .execute() .await?;Putting this design through a real codebase like Kova confirmed something practical: opening up type conversions and capabilities to a user-defined context does more than just get around the Orphan Rule on paper. Even in a complex framework, it keeps dependency boundaries clean, compile times fast, and day-to-day usage comfortable.Rust's Orphan Rule is not there to make life hard. It exists to prevent global implementation conflicts and stop crates from stepping on each other in the global namespace. Once you stop fighting for a "globally unique" implementation and instead leave a generic slot on the trait to scope uniqueness to a local context, bypassing the Orphan Rule takes no black magic at all. It is just a simple shift in perspective, yet it makes both library design and large workspace boundaries much cleaner.In the next post, I will talk about the problem that immediately follows this design: once your traits and query builders carry a generic context parameter, how do you avoid falling into generic type gymnastics and monomorphization bloat? That brings us to boundary validation and type erasure.

This is Rust's well-known Orphan Rule. Once people hit this wall, they usually either complain that the compiler is too rigid or dutifully wrap the type in a NewType. But if you look closely at how the Orphan Rule actually works, it is not a dead end. By design, it leaves a pretty wide door open.What Is the Orphan Rule Actually Protecting Against?Setting the jargon aside, the logic behind the Orphan Rule is simple: if you want a type to implement a trait, at least one of those two things (the type or the trait) must belong to your own crate. In plain English, you don't get to make rules for someone else's types.Suppose crate A implements ToJson for uuid::Uuid and outputs a hyphenated UUID string, while crate B also implements ToJson for uuid::Uuid and outputs 32 raw hex characters without hyphens. If a project depends on both A and B, the compiler has a problem when it sees uuid.to_json(): which implementation should it pick?To prevent this kind of global conflict, Rust enforces coherence, and the Orphan Rule is how it gets enforced.
