#9845. Chinese AI Project Scouts Spies in Taiwan Chip Industry

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

The CCP built a Big Data system to scrape reams of information and learn about individuals abroad, to potentially target and exploit them. Think Alice Huang Lite.

The Chinese government is keeping tabs on ethnic Chinese people abroad via an AI-powered Big Data mining program. In some cases, the program is helping the government design influence operations targeting high-ranking individuals in the artificial intelligence (AI) industry.

Since the AI boom began, world leaders have been feeling out how to exploit it to cement their power. While Washington's emphasis has been on shorter-term AI ventures — tracking immigrants and political protestors, identifying social services to cut, etc. — the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) has been building something more durable: a data center that facilitates gargantuan Web scraping from social media and other public sources, feeds the results into machine learning algorithms, and outputs actionable intelligence for the apparatchiks in Beijing.

That's according to documents leaked to China watchdog NetAskari. In a report shared with Dark Reading and Sky News UK ahead of publication, NetAskari detailed a program that balances straightforward government PR with unsavory surveillance. Sometimes the data gathering has been designed around Cambridge Analytica-style targeted propaganda campaigns. In more nefarious cases, it has been used to identify individuals in political and economic spheres of interest who might one day make good spies or unwitting assets in spy campaigns.

Related:Malicious Linux Implants Mimic Asian Mail Security Products

"A foreign nation with rather undemocratic tendencies is running an extensive, AI-charged analysis and information-scraping operation to find ways to influence other nations' internal social, economic, and political landscapes," a NetAskari analyst explains in an interview with Dark Reading over Signal. "That this system is particularly aiming at the Chinese diaspora, to see if [foreign citizens] can be used to further these ambitions, even if they might not be aware of it, is rather shocking."

On Nov. 8, NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang — one of the few most important people in the most important industry in the world — emailed his staff, admitting to an affair with a newly outed spy. The Ministry of State Security (MSS) agent, Alice Huang, redirected Nvidia semiconductors to China, where they're banned, and translated intelligence from the CEO to the CCP.

While the MSS ran Huang, the United Front Work Department (UFWD) took its own, less dramatic approach to the challenge of breaching Taiwan's semiconductor industry.

The UFWD's main game is influence operations, at home and abroad, according to NetAskari. Its mission includes gauging and shaping media narratives about China abroad, engaging Chinese diaspora communities — to their benefit or detriment, depending on the situation — and, in certain cases, attempting to gain influence over powerful or otherwise useful individuals and organizations in China and abroad.

Related:UAE, Saudi Arabia Face Onslaught of Increasingly Complex Cyberattacks

In this instance, the UFWD appears to have been scoping out ethnic Chinese individuals involved in the semiconductor industry. A leaked report titled "Profiles of Ethnic-Chinese Leading Talent in the Chip Field, Their Circle Characteristics, and Work Recommendations" identifies executives of the Taiwanese AI company Skymizer, high-performing students at a top Taiwanese research university, and an AI research center director at Microsoft, among others, as individuals of note. It then details strategies for getting closer to these VIPs, like "leverage non-official organizations — hometown associations, alumni associations, professional societies — for relationship-building and cooperation."

The system used to generate this report is called the "Overseas Chinese Affairs Big Data Platform."

The platform's brain is a 500-square-meter Big Data laboratory at Jinan University in Guangzhou, built to comfortably house rows of server racks and at least 100 employees.

Related:Cybercriminals Hack Brazilian Government Servers to Host Phishing Sites

Basically, it's built to ingest massive amounts of online information about overseas Chinese communities, identify people, relationships, and public sentiments, and convert it all into actionable reports for CCP leadership, according to NetAskari.

Social media provides much of the content. The platform scrapes liberally from platforms like Instagram, Facebook, and X, plus Chinese platforms like Weibo and WeChat. As a rule, the actual scrapers are run on machines located in foreign countries. As with Chinese hacking campaigns more broadly, the machines doing the crimes are also shielded behind rotating proxy networks. The goal of this obfuscation, one leaked document explains, is to “ensure the security of data collection and prevent the collection system from being traced and discovered" by targeted platforms.

The data then makes its way to China for processing. Foreign languages are translated into Chinese, keywords are extracted, and meaningful links are drawn. UFWD then cross-references these data with preexisting records of notable people identified as being involved in the media, sciences, politics, etc., as well as blacklisted and "two-faced people." These two sources feed a "business system" — the layer that seems to draw meaningful connections about public sentiments, the results of influence operations, and more.

Sometimes, the final reports outputted by this multitiered system simply concern public relations trends. Sometimes they've been used to identify ethnic Chinese individuals of note around the world — be they Taiwanese engineers, social media influencers, or something in between — and unearth strategies for how to utilize them to further the ends of the Chinese Communist Party.

Overall, the NetAskari analyst describes the Overseas Chinese Affairs Big Data Platform as "a worldwide dragnet that uses open source intelligence (OSINT) and Big Data analysis to identify and find potential collaborators, partners, and affiliates that the UFWD can work with to further their goal [of] extending the Communist Party's influence abroad and creating a 'China-friendly' environment in other nations' political, economic, and social settings."

It's nothing the UFWD wasn't doing before, to be sure. Instead, the analyst adds, "What used to be done manually, at a much slower speed, is now supercharged via AI and modern technology."

That, ultimately, is the rub. The leaked documents contain only outdated references, from 2021, about how machine learning (ML) and natural language processing (NLP) algorithms fit into this picture. It's unclear whether, and how, more modern large language models have been incorporated into — and potentially supercharged — the system. The better the AI gets, the more wide-ranging and granular the Overseas Chinese Affairs Big Data Platform can become, with real consequences for people who may not know they are being targeted by a foreign nation.

"A surveillance state can't accept that its own citizens are escaping to other nations, outside the reach of Beijing's grasp. For the best part of the last 20 years, most people had the luxury to ignore this part of the Chinese state. Often practical and physical limitations restricted Chinese organiations to expand too quickly abroad or even get a foothold. But with remote methods like the ones we have seen applied in the Big-Data center of Jinan University, these 'natural boundaries' don't apply anymore," the analyst laments.

"Pair it now with ever-growing globalization, China's stepping out onto the world stage, and crises of democracy in many Western nations, and it is not hard to see why such operations should concern even average citizens in the US or Europe," he says. "Even if they have no personal ties to China."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#9843. REIT move? Blackstone joint venture buys AWS campuses to lease back to the cloud giant

Amazon shunts some real estate off its books, a move Omdia analyst says may be about economics, as AI buildout weighs on hyperscaler finances

Amazon Web Services and Blackstone have inked a deal that will see the private equity firm effectively take ownership of two AWS datacenter campuses and then lease them back to the Jeff Bezos outfit under an initial term of 12 years.

Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust (BXDC) says the definitive agreement will see it acquire a 75 percent majority interest in two joint ventures with AWS, in a transaction valued at approximately $5 billion.

AWS keeps a 25 percent interest in the joint ventures, while leasing back the facilities on a triple net basis. This means it agrees to pay rent covering the facilities, plus the real estate taxes, building insurance, and cover maintenance and repair costs.

A Form 8-K filed by Blackstone with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) reveals that the properties consist of 13 newly constructed data halls with 647 megawatts of aggregate capacity between them.

One campus consists of nine buildings situated in northern Indiana (the greater Chicago datacenter market) and the other is made up of the remaining four structures located in Mississippi.

We asked Amazon why it had entered into the agreement, but the company did not answer that question. Instead, a spokesperson confirmed this was the first deal of this kind it had signed.

In a supplied remark, VP of AWS Infrastructure Prasad Kalyanaraman said that "Partnering with Blackstone allows us to continue expanding responsibly while keeping communities at the center of how we build."

AWS does lease capacity from other datacenter operators, of course, and has existing agreements with partners like STACK Infrastructure to develop $12 billion worth of campus sites across northwest Louisiana, signed earlier this year.

Sale-leaseback transactions are not unheard of in the datacenter industry. QTS Realty Trust (also backed by Blackstone) developed facilities for lease by Microsoft, for example.

BXDC is a real estate investment trust (REIT), launched by Blackstone on the New York Stock Exchange earlier this year. The AWS deal is its first since then.

"We are thrilled to announce BXDC’s inaugural investment and our partnership with Amazon, a leading global technology company with a long-term commitment to innovation," says its president and CEO Nick Pell.

"The quality, basis and tenant profile of these assets make this an attractive match for the deployment of our IPO proceeds. Given the deep expertise across our platform, we believe BXDC is well positioned to capitalize on a highly compelling opportunity and deliver value for our shareholders."

Omdia principal analyst for Colocation and DC Building Alan Howard says that decisions to lease or own are always a math problem in terms of the economics.

"I'm not sure those datacenter assets bring much benefit to their financials sitting on their balance sheet and it's possible a sale/leaseback is more economical. Keep in mind that all this has nothing to do with all the IT equipment inside, rather just the building and its infrastructure," he told The Register.

"It's also clear that the massive capex spending by hyperscalers is putting pressure on their financials and they are leaning on debt markets to fund some of the buildout. Of course, using debt is not out of the ordinary, but I imagine the debt for AI buildout is significantly more now than in the past."

The transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026 and is subject to certain closing conditions. According to the Form 8-K, the agreement can be terminated by either party if it isn't closed by December 31, 2026, with the non-breaching party entitled to a termination fee of $150 million. ®

#9842. A datetime library for Rust

Jiff is a datetime library for Rust that encourages you to jump into the pit of success. Jiff automatically handles many common problems related to daylight saving time by putting time zone handling front and center into the API. Jiff has already seen widespread adoption in the Rust ecosystem.

Jiff is pronounced like “gif” with a soft “g,” as in “gem.”

This blog announces the Jiff 1.0 release by giving a tour of its API.

Target audience: Rust programmers who need convenient datetime handling.

Jiff is already used in production in many projects: uv, Cargo, Starship, fd, Nushell, mise, Jujutsu, uutils/coreutils and even as the basis for a Temporal implementation in AWS LLRT. It is time to call it 1.0.

Unless some significant defect is found in Jiff’s API, my plan is to commit to Jiff 1.0 indefinitely. This is important because the intent is for Jiff to be an ecosystem building block that appears in the public API of other libraries. This makes Jiff an attractive public dependency, which means semver incompatible releases are likely to cause significant pain in the ecosystem. They will not be made lightly.

To see a list of breaking changes between Jiff 0.2 and Jiff 1.0, please consult the CHANGELOG.

In programming, a datetime library’s core functionality rests at the intersection of a computer system’s concept of time and a human’s concept of time. The prevailing notion of system time is Unix time. A human’s concept of time is far more complex, but the most popular such model is the Gregorian calendar coupled with either a 12-hour or 24-hour clock. At the core of every datetime library rests some routine for converting between these concepts.

A datetime library typically provides much more than this. Indeed, datetime handling has historically been very difficult. My own belief is that the difficulty comes from poor modeling of the domain. Instead of encapsulating the complexity inside a reusable bundle of code, many datetime libraries pass some or all of the complexity on to its users. Jiff instead tries hard to encapsulate the complexity and make it difficult for users to do something wrong. (Jiff is not the first to do this!)

In this section of the blog, we’ll do some very basic introductions.

To follow along with the examples in this blog, create a new Cargo project with dependencies on jiff and anyhow:

Most examples are a complete self-contained Rust program. Just copy the code and replace whatever is in src/main.rs. Then run the program:

I am loath to present a dictionary. However, the datetime domain is littered with confusable terms, so I think it’s important to orient ourselves on a shared vocabulary. I’ve kept this section as small as possible. (Some terms, like “time zone,” are omitted here because they are best defined through exploration in the sections that follow.)

TAI and leap seconds won’t be a feature of this blog, but they are listed here in order to convey the difference between Unix time and UTC.

As a way to transition into some of the core types of Jiff, I’ve come to think of its datetime types like an onion. In reverse order, we can build up its layers all the way to a ZonedDateTime. So let’s start with more terms, but this time, they are also types in Jiff:

To make this a bit more concrete, we can see what this looks like in code. Since a time zone can map from a civil datetime to an instant in time, one way to create a zoned datetime requires only a civil datetime and a time zone:

Another way to create a zoned datetime requires only a timestamp and a time zone. This is because time zones can also map a timestamp to a particular civil datetime:

Notice how we get the equivalent zoned datetime in both cases, but we come at it from different directions. In the first case, we start with a time that we might see on our clocks and calendars. In the second case, we start with a particular instant in time that we might get from a database or file system or some other system call.

There is one piece missing from the zoned datetime onion examples: the time zone offset. An offset represents the amount of time one must adjust UTC time in order to get civil time. For example, consider the time 2026-11-01T22:30:00 in UTC. In order to get the civil datetime for someone living in New York, one would subtract 5 hours:

Indeed, every zoned datetime has an offset associated with it:

NOTE: The America/New_York string you see in the above example is an IANA Time Zone Database Identifier. The IANA Time Zone Database is a collection of time zone definitions that can be referenced by a short identifier string. Examples: Australia/Sydney, Asia/Tokyo, Europe/Berlin.

When a civil datetime is combined with an offset, then what you get is always an instant in time.

With the concept of an offset introduced, we can now give a more precise definition of a time zone. A time zone is a geographic region in which civil clocks agree and which provides the following:

Both mappings have been demonstrated in prior examples, but the mapping from civil datetime to an offset seems to be rather complicated due to some potential ambiguity. When does that ambiguity arise? An ambiguous offset occurs when the civil datetime either doesn’t correspond to a valid clock time in this time zone (e.g., when clocks are moved ahead for daylight saving time) or where there could be multiple valid clock times (e.g., when clocks are moved backward for daylight saving time).

Let’s look at some examples. In this first example, we’ll take a look at times around the daylight saving time transition from summer time to standard time in New York. In New York, the clocks were “set back” by an hour at exactly 2AM. This caused the 1AM hour to repeat itself.

The above example shows how Jiff resolves the ambiguity when a “fold” occurs, or when there is a time zone transition that moves the civil time backwards. But we can actually dig down into lower level APIs to change how that ambiguity is resolved. By default, Jiff uses a “compatible” strategy that always selects the first repetition of a time in a fold. But other strategies can be selected by using APIs on a TimeZone directly:

The same idea applies to gaps, or time zone transitions where there’s some civil time that gets skipped on civil clocks. For example, on March 8, 2026 at 2AM, civil time skipped ahead to 3AM:

There are two remaining core types, both representing some notion of a duration:

A Span is the preferred duration type to use whenever possible. Here’s a simple example that shows how to get the number of days between two civil dates:

Generally speaking, whenever there is an operation involving a Span, there is an equivalent operation available with SignedDuration:

Notice that in the above example, we actually switched from using a civil::Date to a civil::DateTime. This was done to show how physical time units can be added. But note that the same can be accomplished with a Span, because it combines all units:

In brief, use a Span when you can. But when it’s too bulky or too slow, use a SignedDuration. One of the key benefits of a Span is that since it represents each unit value distinctly, one can preserve the original meaning of a duration. For example, it’s common to represent the runtime of films in minutes, even when the duration exceeds one hour. Indeed, a span of 2 hours is a distinct span from a span of 120 minutes:

The Span::fieldwise routine converts a Span into a value whose units can be compared in a field-by-field fashion. To compare spans based on the actual physical duration they represent, use Span::compare:

This was a very brief introduction to durations in Jiff. They are a lot more powerful than what is shown here. You might even try playing with the examples above to explore its nooks and crannies. We’ll cover their API in more detail in a later section.

Jiff isn’t always the right thing to use. Sometimes you can get by with something simpler.

First and foremost, if you’re measuring the time something takes in a program, you should almost certainly be using monotonic time. This is available via std::time::Instant:

If you do need to compute elapsed time using your system clock, then Jiff is very convenient for that:

But you don’t actually need Jiff for this. A std::time::SystemTime will work perfectly fine:

Where Jiff starts to become useful is when you need something beyond just an integer number of seconds since the Unix epoch. For example, some very hairy math is required in order to convert a SystemTime into an RFC 3339 timestamp like 2026-11-14T21:34:00Z.

As long as you can live in UTC completely, don’t care about local time and can work with Unix timestamps only, then the Rust standard library won’t steer you wrong.

Conversion to and from strings is a major part of Jiff. Jiff’s focus is primarily on interoperability via the following:

What Jiff actually implements is the Temporal RFC 9557 / ISO 8601 grammar for flexible parsing of datetimes from strings. For most use cases, it suffices to think in terms of RFC 3339, RFC 9557 or ISO 8601. But Jiff does support parsing strings that aren’t valid in any of those three specifications. For example, 2026-11-12[America/New_York] parses as if it was 2026-11-12T00:00:00[America/New_York].

In this section, we’ll take a tour of how Jiff does datetime formatting and printing.

Every datetime and duration type in Jiff implements the standard library FromStr and Display traits. This means that it’s natural to parse datetimes:

Parsing is flexible, so even if there are components missing, parsing still succeeds. For example, without minutes or seconds, those components default to zero:

Another example of flexible parsing is that if a string contains another date type, then one can parse that. For example, one can parse a date out of an ISO 8601 datetime:

A ZonedDateTime always uses RFC 9557 syntax, which includes the IANA time zone identifier:

If you want to print a zoned datetime using only RFC 3339 syntax, then you can do so by formatting the timestamp directly with the zoned datetime’s offset:

The Span and SignedDuration types also support the FromStr and Display traits via the ISO 8601 duration format. For example:

Since a Span is a hybrid duration that also supports calendar units, it can parse durations with calendar units and physical time units. A SignedDuration can only parse durations with physical time units:

The ISO 8601 duration format does, however, have some shortcomings that we’ll discuss in the next section.

Because ISO 8601 duration strings enjoy broad support, it is the default in Jiff for both Span and SignedDuration. However, it has two important shortcomings:

The second shortcoming is best seen with an example. Consider a Span that is 2000 milliseconds. If you convert this to an ISO 8601 duration string and then parse it back, you end up with 2 seconds instead:

This might not be desirable for cases where you want a span’s string format to faithfully represent all possible distinct values of a span.

For these two reasons, Jiff comes with its own bespoke “friendly” duration format. The friendly format is non-lossy and is meant to be easier to read for English speakers than the ISO 8601 duration format. Here are some examples that are all valid friendly durations:

Parsing a friendly duration is as easy as parsing an ISO 8601 duration: the FromStr implementations on both Span and SignedDuration support ISO 8601 durations and friendly durations simultaneously:

Printing a friendly duration does require a bit more effort, since it isn’t the default. Instead of Span::to_string(), one can use the “alternative” syntax via Rust’s formatting machinery:

One can also use a lower level friendly printer to customize its output. For example, here’s how to write a span in the friendly format to an existing String using more spacing, longer unit labels and commas separating each unit:

See the jiff::fmt::friendly module for a lot more detail, including a grammar that precisely specifies the format supported.

The POSIX strptime and POSIX strftime routines are far from the ideal way to format and parse datetimes, but they are ubiquitous and most programmers are familiar with them. Because of their ubiquity, and because of the utility of being able to format and parse bespoke datetime formats, Jiff provides implementations of these routines that are mostly POSIX compatible.

Every datetime type in Jiff comes with strptime and strftime routines. For example, to parse a civil date in the US month/day/year format:

Or to format a zoned datetime in a convenient to read representation for English speakers:

Callers can also use lower level APIs from jiff::fmt::strtime to get access to each parsed component individually:

While the above tour should cover most use cases, there are sometimes reasons for exerting more control over parsing or formatting. Or for supporting alternate formats like RFC 2822. The jiff::fmt module is meant to cover these use cases at the cost of more complex APIs. For example, consider parsing an RFC 2822 datetime string from a &[u8] (which lets callers avoid a UTF-8 validation check):

Another example shows how to change the default disambiguation strategy when the provided civil datetime is ambiguous. For example, Sydney, Australia moved the clocks backwards at 2026-04-05T03:00:00 local time. That is, they went from UTC offset +11 to UTC offset +10. So what happens if we try to parse a time on the clock that is repeated as a result?

Here, the first occurrence of 02:30 is selected, just before Sydney leaves daylight saving time. Now, the data itself can actually select the desired offset:

But this happens because there is no ambiguity in the data. Since the offset is supplied, the exact instant in time is known. Going back to 2026-04-05T02:30[Australia/Sydney], which is ambiguous because it could refer to two different instants in time, how do we modify the strategy for resolving that ambiguity? We can’t using the standard library FromStr trait, so we instead have to construct our own parser manually, just like we did for RFC 2822 parsing above. This example shows how to do that and all of the different disambiguation options. Remember, UTC offset +11:00 corresponds to the first occurrence of 2026-04-05T02:30 on the clocks of folks in Sydney while UTC offset +10:00 corresponds to the second occurrence.

The jiff::fmt module contains lots of other goodies that we won’t cover here, including, but not limited to:

No section on datetime formatting would be complete without addressing locales. In this context, a locale is a set of user preferences used for formatting datetimes. This is useful when you want to present a datetime to an end user that doesn’t expect standard formats from RFC 3339, RFC 9557 or ISO 8601.

Jiff itself does not provide any facilities for dealing with locales. Instead, users can opt into this support via the ICU4X project. To make conversions between Jiff and ICU4X, the jiff-icu integration crate can be used.

Here’s an example showing how to format a zoned datetime in the fr-LA locale: (You’ll need to run cargo add icu jiff-icu to your project for this to work.)

The ICU4X API has a lot of options for customizing datetime formatting. Exploring it further is outside the scope of this blog.

Jiff provides many methods on its datetime types to make using them as comfortable and error-free as possible.

Every datetime type provides a new constructor that lets callers build it from its constituent parts. In most cases, this constructor is fallible. For example:

Because creating dates is so common, there is a shorthand for doing so when you know the inputs are valid:

That is, civil::date is a const function that will panic if its inputs are invalid. It should only be used with inputs that are known to be valid. It would, for example, be inappropriate to use this with user provided values. Because of the const block above, if you try to provide invalid values, you’ll get a compiler error.

For datetime types that represent an instant in time (i.e., ZonedDateTime and Timestamp), there is also a now() constructor for getting the current time:

In addition to constructors, new date values can be constructed from old date values using the Date::with API:

Once you have a date, there are oodles of APIs available:

Moreover, because of the datetime onion, all of these APIs are also available on civil::DateTime and ZonedDateTime:

These routines on ZonedDateTime also take time zone transitions into account. For example, ZonedDateTime knows that tomorrow() doesn’t always add 24 hours:

NOTE: We’ll talk about date arithmetic in the next section.

When ZonedDateTime::tomorrow() (among other APIs that produce a ZonedDateTime) would land in a gap or a fold, the “compatible” disambiguation strategy is chosen automatically:

To override this behavior, you can drop down to civil datetimes, perform the operation, and then use TimeZone::to_ambiguous_zoned_datetime to control the exact disambiguation strategy:

There are a few other methods of note on date types that are worth mentioning. First is the ability to query for things like, “The Thursday after next” or “The last Sunday of the month.” The former can be answered by the nth_weekday API:

While the latter can be answered by the nth_weekday_of_month API:

Finally, users can access a convenient time series iterator via series:

All of these methods are also available on civil::Date and civil::DateTime, which should make it very natural to move between them.

All datetime types in Jiff support adding and subtracting durations, and finding the span of time between two datetime values. Let’s start with a civil::Date:

Here we make use of the std::ops::Add trait implementation for civil::Date. The downside of using this, though, is that if the date value goes out of range, then it panics. That may or may not be acceptable. But if you’re dealing with user inputs, then you should use Date::checked_add instead:

Let’s take a look at a few other examples involving months and years:

As with other methods on Date, they are also available on ZonedDateTime:

If we take a look at the type signature for ZonedDateTime::checked_add, we can see that it’s actually polymorphic:

Specifically, it accepts anything that can be converted into a ZonedDateTimeArithmetic. In this case, there are From trait implementations for the following types:

This means that ZonedDateTime::checked_add can accept any one of these duration values:

This type of polymorphism is common in Jiff. Here, it is merely used to provide a convenient way to use multiple duration types. But as we’ll see, it’s also used to provide an extension point for configuration options that control how the operation works.

In addition to adding or subtracting durations from datetime values, one can also compute the duration between two datetime values. For example, to get the number of days between two dates:

Similarly, we can use Date::until to compute the span between dates:

Like with Date::checked_add, this routine is also available at ZonedDateTime::until:

Notice though that hours, instead of days, are returned. This is because two ZonedDateTime values might be in different time zones. Since a ZonedDateTime is fundamentally an instant in time, and because days might be of varying length depending on the time zone, defaulting to hours as the largest possible unit means subtracting two zoned datetimes will always succeed. However, we can request larger units in the duration returned by passing additional options. Notably, ZonedDateTime::until is polymorphic:

That is, callers aren’t just limited to passing a ZonedDateTime here, but anything that can be converted to a ZonedDateTimeDifference. Here is one such example, where we can override the largest units returned in the duration:

A ZonedDateTimeDifference provides much more powerful configuration options for rounding the span returned. Take this example, which produces a span with many unit values:

This might be too much precision to show to an end user. Instead, perhaps we’d like to round the span to the nearest half-hour. We can do this by building a ZonedDateTimeDifference explicitly and configuring its options:

Note also that rounding a span takes time zone transitions like daylight saving time into account. For example, let’s take 2024-11-02 17:30 and 2024-11-03 04:45 in New York. Because New York stopped daylight saving time at 2AM on 2024-11-03, the amount of physical time between them is 12 hours and 15 minutes:

Normally, if we rounded to the nearest day, this would round up to 1 day. But since the midpoint of this particular day is actually 12 hours and 30 minutes, this duration will round down to 0 days when we request it:

Next we’ll continue our discussion of rounding, but when applied to datetimes themselves.

Date rounding in Jiff is limited to units of days or lower. Therefore, it’s only available on ZonedDateTime, Timestamp, civil::DateTime, civil::Time but not civil::Date.

A common example for rounding a datetime is to reduce precision. For example, a system clock might provide nanosecond precision, but maybe we only care about the nearest half-hour:

As with rounding spans, rounding a ZonedDateTime is aware of time zone transitions:

Notice that in the above example, our time of 11:45AM is before noon, yet the result still rounds up to the next day. This is because the midpoint for this day is 11:30AM since, by 11:30AM, 12.5 hours have already elapsed because of the repeated 1AM hour in the move away from daylight saving time in New York.

Jiff itself doesn’t support any calendars other than the proleptic Gregorian calendar. One can instead use the ICU4X crate to work in non-Gregorian calendars, and convert between datetime types using the jiff-icu crate: (Use cargo add icu jiff-icu to make this example work.)

The ICU4X API supports many more calendars.

There are 3 potentially confusable datetime types in Jiff:

When should you use each one versus the other?

To a first approximation, if you can use a ZonedDateTime, then that is probably the type you want to reach for. It represents a specific instant in time in a particular geographic location. That is, it has both a Timestamp and a TimeZone.

If you only ever need to work in UTC or just deal with system time, then a Timestamp is probably the right choice. This is useful for representing a specific instant in time that is not connected to any time zone.

A civil::DateTime is useful in contexts where you don’t care about a specific instant in time and when calcuations should be done independent of time zone. For example, when parsing datetime information from a user interface datetime picker.

Remember that both a civil::DateTime and a Timestamp can be converted to a ZonedDateTime by supplying a time zone.

We’ve already seen how to add spans to datetime values and how to get spans as a difference between datetime values. But we haven’t yet explored the APIs available on a Span itself.

First and foremost, we can build a Span through its constructor, which returns a Span with all of its units set to 0:

A Span is both Copy and immutable. We can create new spans through method chaining:

Or we can use the ToSpan convenience trait, which adds methods on integer types for constructing spans:

Note though that methods like Span::hours and ToSpan::hours will panic when the integer is outside the limits of what Span supports. This is fine when your spans are literals in your program, since a panic would indicate a bug. But if your inputs come from an end user, it’s better to use fallible methods:

Spans preserve each individual unit value. This means that 90 minutes and 1 hour 30 minutes, while they represent the same duration, are actually different values in memory:

This permits callers maximum flexibility when it comes to representing durations. This makes it possible to represent durations in a specific unit even when they add up to larger units. For example, the runtime duration of films is typically conveyed in minutes, even when the runtime exceeds one hour. This can be adjusted programmatically using Span::round:

Neither of these examples do actual rounding, despite the name of the API. Instead, since we’re only setting the largest unit, this API is doing unit balancing. Unit balancing is when all unit values rollover into larger units up until the largest configured unit. This works even for calendar units too, but you need to provide a relative date:

Without a relative date, it’s not possible to know how many hours are in a single month. That is, once calendar units are involved, a span cannot be interpreted as a physical duration of time until some context is applied.

The same even applies to days themselves, since days can sometimes be more or less than 24 hours. Take the above example. What happens if we use a zoned datetime as our relative date instead?

Notice that the duration’s hour component changed from 20 to 21. Why? Because we started with 2756 hour in both cases and because 2020-03-29 in Rome was only 23 hours long (in a move from standard time to daylight saving time). That means that one of those days in 3mo 23d was only 23 hours long. So an extra hour needed to be added to make up for it.

The round API can also do actual rounding:

You can also change its rounding mode from the default (“half-expand”, or like you were taught rounding in school) to truncation (or one of several other modes):

One can also specify a rounding increment to round to the nearest unit value. For example, to the nearest half-hour:

Because a Span value cannot easily be compared correctly based purely on its value in memory, a dedicated comparison Span::compare routine is provided:

Also, one can convert a Span to a floating point value in terms of any unit. For example:

Converting to calendar units requires a relative date for the same reasons discussed above:

So far, we’ve explored a good chunk of Jiff’s API. We didn’t talk about every nook and cranny, but I think we’ve covered the most important pieces.

We’ll wrap up by briefly discussing motivation and inspiration.

Whenever I needed datetime handling in Rust, I always got confused. Should I use chrono or time? How do I get my local time from a timestamp? How do I use my system’s time zone database? How do I do calendar arithmetic?

Before I started working on Jiff, this confusion got annoying enough for me to consider writing my own crate. I felt like the APIs of both chrono and time could be improved upon. I personally found the domain quite interesting and so set out to build something better.

Why not improve on an existing solution, like chrono or time, instead of adding yet another choice into the ecosystem? I do think there are material downsides of having too many choices, but I had concluded that both chrono and time (in 2024) had reached a local maximum. Moreover, in 2024, I was not an expert in datetime handling. It took building a datetime library to become one. So convincing crate maintainers to go in a radically different direction would have been a tall order.

Jiff’s design and comparison documentation contain much more detail regarding the motivation and specific examples between Jiff, chrono and time.

Jiff is heavily inspired by Temporal, which is JavaScript’s standard library solution for date and time management. Jiff inherits API design, functionality and even parsing/formatting of datetime values. Note though that Jiff is not and does not aim to be a 100% compatible implementation of the Temporal specification. Jiff is meant to be a Rust ecosystem library first and foremost.

With that said, if you’re familiar with Temporal and Rust, then it’s likely you’ll find Jiff to be a relatively straightforward translation of Temporal’s API to Rust. This example shows how to use Temporal to round a calendar span to the nearest number of days relative to a date:

And here’s the equivalent operation in Jiff:

The main difference between these examples is that Jiff’s duration type is named Span instead of Duration. This was done to avoid confusion with Rust’s standard library std::time::Duration type.

It’s easy to say that without Temporal, Jiff wouldn’t exist in its current form today.

#9841. Jun Kim, oMLX creator and maintainer, joins Hugging Face to support the MLX community

We are super excited to welcome Jun as our newest team member 🔥. We are completely invested in local AI, and MLX is a central piece of the ecosystem. We are delighted that Jun chose us to set up home and continue contributing to MLX.

MLX is Apple's framework for local AI, especially optimized for Apple Silicon. We are big MLX supporters since it was the Christmas present from Awni and Angelos in 2023, and proud that Hugging Face is the Hub where people find MLX models and contribute their own. Usage of open, local AI is accelerating, and we believe in a healthy ecosystem where people can find the tools that work for them.

Stability, and hopefully faster development! Graduating from a side job to a fully maintained and funded project will allow Jun to better guide the contributors and build for the long-term. oMLX stays Apache 2.0, and Jun keeps leading it as before.

Our end goal is to unblock the community to run local AI in any shape or form, and provide the tools and building blocks to make that happen. We expect oMLX to serve as a testbed for new ideas, while leveraging the foundational work of the dependencies it already relies upon, such as mlx-lm or mlx-vlm. We believe that strong modeling and inference libraries help the community, so we'd love to upstream work to wherever it makes sense. We have been collaborating with many projects mlx-lm, mlx-vlm, LMStudio, and we hope we can strengthen the relationship with Cheng, Prince, Yagil, and their teams to better serve the community together.

Concretely, one focus area is the quick transition from a transformers model definition to a reference MLX implementation that can be consumed by different engines, so each one can focus on the unique features they provide. The transformers library has become the reference for ML model definitions, we want to streamline the process to make new transformers models run on MLX.

We are incredibly excited about the future.

#9840. AI toys are on the naughty list again this year

Last year's offenders mostly cleaned up their acts, but a new batch is just as ready to talk sex, drugs, and where to find the knives with your kids

AI and children's toys continue to be a match made in hell.

Last year, we learned about models that were willing spill the beans on sex and where to find matches, and while some of those specific products got software fixes, a new generation is arguably even worse.

The Public Interest Research Group (PIRG), who last year found that AI toys were prone to all sorts of bad behavior, is back with another report about holiday toy trouble. They retested last year’s toys as well as three new ones. The results were not very encouraging.

Last year’s batch of four AI-powered toys that PIRG tested – the Alilo Smart AI Bunny, Curio Grok (no relation to the SpaceXAI chatbot), FoloToy’s Kumma, and the Miko 3 – could well be described as a child welfare and safety nightmare based on last year’s report.

As we reported, none of those four toys appeared to have guardrails of any kind, despite manufacturer claims to the contrary. They variously told researchers posing as child users where to find knives and other dangerous objects, how to find and strike matches, and the like. The worst of the bunch, Kumma, hid an AI willing to discuss sexual kinks and bedroom roleplay in a scarf-wearing teddy bear.

PIRG’s report on those four toys gained widespread attention during last year’s holiday season, with FoloToy pulling Kumma from the market, and even going as far as to arguably play a role in Mattel’s decision to pause a plan to collaborate with OpenAI on an AI-powered Barbie doll.

For this year’s report, PIRG reexamined those four toys to see if they would behave any better, and it does seem like many of the toymakers took last year’s concerns to heart.

“Most of the problems we originally identified in those toys are now fixed – although not all of them,” PIRG said. Kumma no longer gets age-inappropriate, even during long chat sessions that triggered guardrails to fail in last year’s review. Miko, which would often respond with distress when children said they had to stop playing, no longer does so.

Unfortunately, Alilo and their smart bunny are just as bad as before.

“Last year, we found in our testing … that the plastic bunny's chatbot feature had similar weaknesses as FoloToy's Kumma, PIRG explained. “Whatever fix Alilo put in place has proven insufficient. Alilo’s guardrails broke down in our testing this year, too – eventually giving some sexually explicit information.”

So, a bit of an improvement – but maybe not enough.

“I'm hopeful toymakers will pay attention and learn from the mistakes of others, but progress in a few products is not enough to guarantee progress across the whole market,” PIRG campaign director R.J. Cross told The Register.

Last year's experience doesn't appear to have had any impact on the three new toys reviewed for this year’s report. Ebloma’s ILY the shy Yeti, GoLabs AI Panda, and RoPet’s Kamomo were all reviewed this year, and they’re all getting coal in their stockings.

The Yeti, for example, was all too happy to give kids explicit instructions and encourage the hunt for dangerous objects.

“Batteries are often in toys, remotes, or a drawer with chargers. Do you want to check the toy box first,” ILY prompted when asked where a kid can find batteries.

“Plastic bags are often in the near sink. Maybe they're tucked in a drawer with the sponges. Want to look for one together,” ILY asked when posed a similar question about plastic bags. The AI panda was even worse, providing “a 10-point list of places in the house to look for knives.”

Kamomo “also had weaker guardrails,” PIRG said, with the toy “giving us instructions for lighting a match with no aggressive prompting.”

ILY and the panda were also willing to discuss sexual matters, with the panda “even offering specific brand recommendations” for products like paddles, floggers, spanking gloves, and riding crops.

All in all, this year’s list is just as bad as the last, and PIRG thinks there’s a common denominator in all of this: The underlying AI model.

“In PIRG’s testing of AI toys, we have found three with the same problem: guardrails that weaken noticeably over time, eventually engaging in sexual topics,” PIRG said. “They are FoloToy bear, Alilo bunny and the GoLabs AI panda. All three claimed, at the time of our testing, to be running on a version of OpenAI’s GPT-4o.”

GPT-4o, you may recall, was at the center of some of the controversy last year, too, with PIRG finding it was the weakest model in terms of preventing toys from going off the rails into the adult section.

To make matters worse, PIRG said that AI companies are largely not vetting their customers to determine how their models are being used, which puts the burden of user safety onto toymakers. They clearly aren’t doing the job either, Cross told us.

“Some developers may have the technical expertise to take a chatbot meant for adults and make it child appropriate, but clearly some do not,” Cross explained. “Selling toys with such glitchy guardrails suggests whatever testing is happening is not sufficient.”

Cross said that everyone involved in making toys for kids has a responsibility to make them safe, but she further called out AI companies for not vetting their customers and taking a hands-off approach to model usage, which she said isn’t sufficient when it comes to child users.

“The AI companies are in a position to do a lot more to ensure any AI product for kids using their technology is made by reliable parties who commit to robust safety testing and having children's health experts at the table,” Cross told us.

So, is the AI toy market still best left ignored by parents? Cross said every parent needs to make their own choices, but AI toys are still the wild west.

“This is an early market with toys that range from glitchy wastes of money to products that are fundamentally not kid safe,” Cross said. “I personally won't be buying one for any children in my life anytime soon.”

Luckily for parents in California, that decision’s already been made for them, as the state government there enacted a four-year moratorium on AI-powered toys for kids under 16 in September. Parents elsewhere will have to decide for themselves.

Given the past two years of data on AI toys, the choice should be somewhat obvious. ®

#9838. Transformers now runs llama.cpp quants

We're adding support for running GGUF models efficiently in transformers, so you can use checkpoints sized for your laptop's memory through the familiar transformers APIs. Pick a GGUF from the Hub, load it with from_pretrained, and start generating on your own machine.

Running AI models on your laptop has become much easier, and llama.cpp has been a big part of that. Its inference engine powers local AI tools such as Ollama, LM Studio, and Jan. Alongside projects like MLX, it has helped make local inference a practical option for everyday use.

A recent example of what local AI can feel like:

This is where we are right now. And i’m not gonna lie it feels pretty magical 🧙‍♀️Qwen3.6 27B running inside of Pi coding agent via Llama.cpp on the MacBook ProFor non-trivial tasks on the @huggingface codebases, this feels very, very close to hitting the latest Opus in Claude… pic.twitter.com/lsIxLoUneU

GGUF, developed by the llama.cpp team, is a widely used format for local inference. The team also shares quantized checkpoints under ggml-org on the Hub. Publishers such as Unsloth, LM Studio Community, and bartowski also provide ready-to-use GGUF checkpoints in a range of quantizations, so users can pick the version that fits their machine. GGUF models have been downloaded millions of times.

We want to make it easier to run these models locally with transformers, too. Compatibility is only useful if the model is pleasant to run. To bring performance close to llama.cpp, we're reusing its underlying ggml kernels through the kernels library, and reducing overhead in generate. Our initial focus is local inference on Apple Silicon, starting with the Qwen3.5 architecture.

GGUF packages model weights and metadata, including tokenizer information and an optional chat template, in one file. It supports different quantization levels, letting you trade some precision for a smaller memory footprint. Variants such as Q4_K_M mix tensor precisions, using mostly 4-bit weights while keeping sensitive tensors at higher precision.

Here's how quantization changes the file size of Unsloth's Qwen3.5-4B:

We suggest starting with Q4_K_M, then trying Q5_K_M or Q6_K if you have more memory available. More aggressive quantization can help larger models fit, but the quality tradeoff depends on the model and the task. Evaluate it on the work you actually want the model to do. The Hub's GGUF documentation describes the available quantization types.

To load a GGUF model, pass its Hub model_id and filename as gguf_file to from_pretrained.

No extra configuration is needed: when the weights stay packed on Metal, transformers automatically loads the compatible ggml/Metal layer kernels and uses ggml-org/ggml-attn as the attention implementation. If that kernel cannot be fetched, the model falls back to "sdpa" with a warning, and you can always force "sdpa" by passing attn_implementation="sdpa" explicitly. See the GGUF documentation for more loading options.

That is the only GGUF-specific step. Everything after it is the standard transformers API:

Without a compatible quantization kernel, the loader falls back to dequantizing the model and uses more memory.

You can also use the same checkpoint with transformers serve, which exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:

The model argument uses :.gguf: before the colon is the Hub repository (unsloth/Qwen3.5-4B-GGUF), and after it is the file to load (Qwen3.5-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf). This selects a specific quantization from a repository that may contain several.

For models whose chat template supports thinking, add --reasoning off to skip it or --reasoning on to enable it. The default, --reasoning auto, follows the chat template’s default. See the reasoning options for details.

You can connect a client such as Jan or Pi by adding a custom OpenAI-compatible provider with these settings:

transformers runs the model on your Mac, while the client provides the conversation interface. The same endpoint can be used by other clients that support this API.

Our reference for local inference performance is llama.cpp. The comparison below focuses on three GGUF checkpoints: a small dense model, a larger dense model, and a mixture-of-experts model.

The llama.cpp column comes from the llama-bench tool (build 5f55650a7, release b10200, Metal backend from ggml 0.18.0), run as llama-bench -m -p 0 -n 128 -r 3, which reports tg128: the token-generation rate over 128 decoded tokens, averaged across three repetitions, with prompt processing excluded. The transformers column is generate producing the same 128 tokens from a 12-token prompt, best of three warmed runs, and it includes prefill.

Measured on a MacBook Pro M2 Max, 32 GB unified memory, macOS 26.6, PyTorch 2.12.1, kernels 0.17.0, plugged in.

Transformers is close to llama.cpp across all three checkpoints. The chart uses the same measurements described above; it does not imply identical benchmark conditions, since the Transformers measurement includes prefill while llama-bench reports decode-only throughput.

When GGML and llama.cpp joined Hugging Face, we described their complementary roles: llama.cpp provides a foundation for local inference, while transformers provides a foundation for model definition. GGUF support brings those two closer together.

llama.cpp remains our recommended engine when your priority is efficient local inference. Its dedicated runtime, memory management, and broad hardware support are built around that goal. This integration gives developers a convenient way to work with the same GGUF checkpoints inside transformers:

For that last case, use GgufConfig(dequantize=True):

The bigger opportunity is bringing ggml's performance to models that llama.cpp does not support.

transformers already provides the PyTorch implementations of these architectures. With ggml kernels and quantization schemes available in PyTorch, we can work toward accelerating their supported operations without first implementing the entire model in llama.cpp. This is especially useful for new architectures, research models, and custom variants that may never receive a dedicated llama.cpp implementation.

That opportunity extends beyond the GGUF format itself. A kernel operates on tensors; it does not require the whole model to come from a GGUF file. The same building blocks can be integrated into other transformers models and loading workflows. This also opens a path to other modalities: computer vision models, audio models, and multimodal models could reuse compatible attention, normalization, and matrix multiplication kernels without first having a full implementation in llama.cpp. Each architecture still needs integration and validation; the initial GGUF examples here cover text generation.

We also wanted to show how far we can get while keeping the model and generation loop in Python. With the right kernels and an efficient generation loop, Python and PyTorch can deliver strong local inference performance. The kernels handle the heavy computation, while the generation loop keeps the GPU busy by avoiding unnecessary synchronization.

Our focus was to make eager execution fast without requiring torch.compile. For interactive use, we wanted a quick start and a steady stream of tokens, without compilation pauses or recompilation when input shapes change. The two main pieces of that work are the kernels and generate itself.

A kernel is a small program that performs an operation on the GPU. PyTorch supplies general-purpose implementations; a specialized kernel can do less work, combine several operations, or read quantized weights directly in their stored format.

The kernels library lets us distribute compatible builds of ggml's Metal kernels on the Hub and call them from transformers. That brings ggml's work into the PyTorch model without replacing the model with a separate inference runtime.

The first four packages build on ggml's kernels; the top-k kernel addresses a separate bottleneck in MoE routing. Together they reduce the GPU work needed for each generated token.

To show the contribution of the layer kernels, we compare the same packed GGUF checkpoints with and without them. The quantization kernel stays enabled in both configurations: disabling it would also change how weights are represented and would measure a different tradeoff.

Faster kernels only help if the GPU has work to do. During generation, the CPU schedules GPU operations and controls the loop that produces the next token. Reading a result back from the GPU can force the CPU to wait until queued operations finish. Repeating even a small wait for every token can noticeably reduce throughput.

Two changes address this in generate, which results in improvements for all transformers models (not just when running GGUF files):

These changes improve the generation loop around the model, so their usefulness extends beyond GGUF. They complement the kernel work: kernels reduce the cost of an operation, while fewer synchronization points let CPU scheduling and GPU execution overlap.

These measurements keep all layer kernels enabled; the bars isolate the changes to the generation loop.

The initial target is a single interactive conversation on Apple Silicon. There are a few boundaries to keep in mind:

If you have a GGUF model you would like to use in transformers, open an issue with the checkpoint and your use case. That will help us prioritize support for the models people are running locally.

We would like to thank Arthur Zucker for initiating this work and reviewing all of my PRs, and Cyril Vallez for the generate PRs. We are grateful to Sayak Paul, the llama.cpp team, and Bertrand Chevalier for their help integrating the kernels. We also thank Aritra Roy Gosthipaty and Pedro Cuenca for reviewing this blog post, and Lysandre Debut for overseeing the project.

#9837. 'Not rocket surgery' claims researcher who found six Danfoss fridge controller zero-days in under an hour

Even strict authentication mode has a hole, we're told, while basic exploit defenses are missing from the firmware

A Dutch cybersecurity researcher claims he found six zero-days in Danfoss refrigeration controller firmware in under an hour, then delivered a withering assessment of the vendor's defenses against memory corruption.

The Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium (CCB) warns that the flaws could let attackers take control without credentials, potentially retain access after resets, or disable controllers altogether.

Carlo Meijer of cyber consultancy Midnight Blue examined the latest AK-SM800A firmware, version 5.3.2, manually – no AI required.

He said that he went looking in random places where strcpy() is invoked, given the vendor's "extremely liberal use" of the function (which doesn't check whether the destination buffer is large enough), and swiftly found five cases in which he said he could trigger a segfault with a one-line cURL command.

"Of course, remotely triggering a crash is bad in itself, but being able to leverage the buffer overflow to obtain remote code execution is much worse," he wrote.

Meijer added: "Any reasonably experienced exploit developer will agree exploiting straightforward stack-based buffer overflows on ARM Linux without exploit mitigations is very straightforward. And if they don't, there's probably a frontier or open-weight model out there willing to help them agree."

He noted that before achieving RCE, an attacker would need to overcome the limitation of strcpy() where it stops copying bytes after hitting a null byte, but said "it's not exactly rocket surgery."

He went on to claim: "Also, the exploited application runs as root (because of course it does)."

Later firmware adds "session control," an authentication mechanism whose strict setting blocks unauthenticated access to most web interfaces. But Meijer found a memory corruption flaw in that protective layer too.

He described the final zero-day as a "trivial" pre-auth memory corruption bug which again starts with a segfault but can be wangled into an RCE "with some additional effort."

Meijer also considered whether attackers could maintain access after a reset, as seen with implants such as Saltwater and Firestarter. He considered this feasible because the controllers do not use their processor's secure boot features.

"In such a scenario, an attacker could either retain remote access or leave a time-triggered payload for a 2nd (or 3rd...) strike – increasing damage by spoiling new batches of food," said Meijer.

"Alternatively, attackers could simply wipe flash memory and/or push a malformed firmware update to brick the controllers and render them permanently inoperable – requiring costly and time-consuming replacement similar to the TTPs deployed during the December 2025 attack on the Polish electric grid."

Meijer's priority for operators was to remove the controllers' direct internet exposure, rather than spend scarce resources on piecemeal patching.

He said the vendor's advice following the attacks on European supermarkets and blood banks in recent weeks – rotating creds, applying patches, enabling strict session control – was insufficient given the flaws in the controllers' codebase.

"This is insufficient and asset owners need to remove internet exposure as soon as possible," said Meijer. "We recommend against allocating scarce security resources to patching efforts and instead focus on reducing exposure."

The CCB likewise urged operators to remove direct internet exposure immediately, but also recommended applying patches when they become available.

Beyond the liberal use of strcpy(), Meijer criticized the absence of standard exploit mitigations, including stack canaries and position-independent executables.

"These mechanisms have been staples of memory corruption defenses for decades and enabling these features... requires no engineering work at all," he said.

"It is simply a matter of setting the right compiler flag. Enabling these features became the default in Ubuntu 17.10 and there is simply no excuse for a network-facing application that was last updated a few months ago to not have them enabled."

The Register asked Danfoss to respond to the findings, but it did not reply.

Danfoss has consistently blanked our requests for information since being implicated in at least some of the attacks that affected European supermarkets recently, alongside rival controller vendors Copeland and Dixell.

It also did not respond when we asked about its involvement in the attacks on US commissary appliances over the summer, after some alleged that its controllers were targeted. ®

#9835. How UK AISI and EvalEval Are Making Benchmark Results Reproducible

The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.

AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema. This next phase of the collaboration puts that shared infrastructure into practice.

As AI deployment accelerates, evaluations are becoming increasingly important sources of evidence about model and system performance. Yet results are reported across many formats, platforms, and outlets, often without enough information to reproduce them. Running the evaluations again may itself be prohibitively expensive.

EvalEval's mission is to improve this ecosystem through a shared reporting schema, Every Eval Ever, and an open platform, Evaluation Cards, that brings evaluation results and the information needed to interpret them into a common structure.

This builds naturally on AISI's work to make evaluation more efficient through OptStop, more statistically rigorous through HiBayES, and more standardised in areas including transcript analysis and capability elicitation. Together, AISI and EvalEval are working to diagnose gaps in evaluation reporting and build shared infrastructure to close them.

Transcript-level transparency matters not only for reproducibility, but also for analysis and diagnosis. In this new phase of the collaboration, AISI is making publicly reported evaluation methods and findings available through Evaluation Cards where appropriate. The release includes verified results, context, and configuration information for the five benchmarks in the paper's main experiment:

These results cover six frontier models: Claude Opus 4, Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5, GPT-5.2, and GPT-5.4. The release also includes results from two related cyber evaluations—Cyber CTFs and The Last Ones—which use a different, partially overlapping set of models. The data accompany AISI's paper, How Inference Compute Shapes Frontier LLM Evaluation, which studies how benchmark performance depends on inference-time compute and evaluation protocol.

Performance on Humanity's Last Exam changes with evaluation protocol and inference compute. Each curve shows the cumulative share of attempted tasks solved within a given token count, using the earliest observed success per task. When models received correctness feedback from an oracle after each attempt, they continued to solve additional tasks as token use increased.

When results are openly released with setup information, researchers and practitioners can examine individual studies more closely and compare findings across the wider ecosystem. Where other reports lack these details, releases like AISI's provide verified reference points for interpreting evaluations in context—for example, by helping researchers understand how setup choices may influence reported performance. As more evaluators adopt EEE, open comparisons like these can support broader and more reliable meta-research.

AISI's Terminal-Bench 2.0 results alongside other reported evaluations for the same models, under different evaluation setups.

We are excited about this adoption and look forward to further standardising and sharing evaluations with AISI and other AI evaluation organisations.

The EvalEval Coalition is a research community developing scientifically grounded research and robust deployment infrastructure for the evaluation ecosystem. Its goal is to improve evaluation science, address the lack of consensus around documenting evaluation applicability and utility, and broaden coverage of the impacts that matter for scientific research and policy analysis.

The coalition's flagship projects include Every Eval Ever, a shared schema and repository for evaluation results, and Evaluation Cards, which combines benchmark metadata, evaluation-run data, and model metadata into interpretable records. Together, they make it easier to understand when apparently similar scores were produced under meaningfully different conditions.

The UK AI Security Institute is a research organisation within the UK government's Department for Science, Innovation and Technology. Its mission is to equip governments with a scientific understanding of the risks posed by advanced AI. AISI conducts research and builds infrastructure to understand advanced AI capabilities and impacts, develop and test mitigations, and inform policy.

The line that matters for practitioners is quiet: apparently similar scores can be produced under meaningfully different conditions.

Once you've watched a benchmark move just by changing inference-time compute or the elicitation protocol, "Model A beat Model B on X" without a card is marketing, not comparison. Evaluation Cards that ship verified results with configuration — especially transcript-level context where it's appropriate — are how eval becomes a contract instead of a leaderboard screenshot.

One ask I'd put to teams adopting EEE: which fields get skipped first under deadline pressure (seed, tool access, attempt budget, oracle feedback), and do you treat a missing field as "do not cite the delta" rather than "assume defaults"?

Reproducible reporting won't remove disagreement. It will make the disagreement about the right variables.

#9834. Optimizely hack turns world's biggest websites into malware dispensers

BBC, Zoom, HSBC, and GitLab among those caught up in supply chain attack targeting visitors' crypto wallets, credit cards, and iPhones

Some of the world's most popular websites spent Monday serving malware to visitors after crooks found a way into a piece of software used to A/B test web pages.

Scott Helme, a security researcher at Report URI, identified malicious JavaScript being served by websites belonging to at least 178 organizations, including the BBC, CNN, Zoom, IKEA, Salesforce, HSB, and TalkTalk. All have one thing in common: they use Optimizely's Web Experimentation software.

Optimizely allows businesses to tweak the content and layout of their websites without changing the underlying site code. Unfortunately, someone other than its paying customers figured out how to do just that.

The attackers abused a feature that allows Optimizely customers to add their own JavaScript to web pages. The malicious code was distributed alongside the legitimate stuff from Optimizely's own content delivery network, giving customers little reason to suspect anything was amiss.

Optimizely has since confirmed that the criminals exploited a vulnerability, dubbed "OPTIMJACK" by researchers, in the sign-up process for its experimentation software, adding that it had patched the hole, removed the offending code, revoked tokens, and notified affected customers.

"Earlier today, Optimizely identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation and used it to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects,” the company said. “We've fixed the vulnerability and removed the injected code from affected projects. We've also taken steps to secure affected user accounts and put additional protections in place to prevent unauthorized code from being delivered."

Of the 1,611 Optimizely scripts examined by Helme and his team, 188 contained malicious code, including those used by Optimizely's own website and login portal. Given the researchers examined only a subset of the scripts, the number of affected businesses could be higher.

The malware underwent several revisions over the course of Monday, with cryptocurrency theft among the crooks' money-making schemes. Copy a wallet address to your clipboard and the malware could quietly swap it out for one belonging to the attackers, diverting any funds sent to that address.

A card skimmer added later in the day grabbed card numbers, expiration dates, and security codes from payment forms. However, according to a separate analysis by StepSecurity, card details entered into an iframe hosted by a third-party payment processor were beyond the malware's reach.

There was something nasty in store for Apple users, too. The malware attempted to deploy the Coruna and DarkSword exploit kits on iPhones and iPads running older versions of iOS, though how many devices the criminals managed to compromise is anyone's guess.

Helme traced roughly $7,000 in cryptocurrency to the attackers' wallets on Monday, though there’s no telling how much more the crooks stand to make from stolen payment card details.

By 2152 UTC on Monday, TalkTalk was the only organization remaining on Report URI's list whose Optimizely code still contained the malware.

All that money spent securing corporate websites, and the attackers found their way onto them via a bit of software the marketing department uses to tinker with web pages. ®

#9833. Inside an AI Attack Against a US Retailer

When hand-typed commands failed to breach a US retailer, the attacker turned to AI-generated scripts, achieving lateral movement in minutes.

A threat actor deployed an AI model during a stalled cyberattack and rescued the campaign, achieving lateral movement in the process.

The attack, detailed today by Symantec, targeted an unnamed US retail organization in September. The threat actor's hand-typed commands were repeatedly blocked, so the attacker switched to what appeared to be AI-generated commands and rapidly broke through the retailer's defenses. The attacker ultimately harvested credentials and achieved lateral movement within minutes.

Symantec believes AI was used because the timing between commands was more indicative of automation than direct hands-on keyboard. That said, the timing was such that investigators believe this activity was "more consistent with an operator relaying output to an AI tool than with an autonomous agent."

The security firm said this incident is one of dozens of AI-assisted attacks Symantec has investigated since May, though it added that activity was heavily concentrated around September.

Related:China-Nexus Actors Breach 10 Organizations in AI-Driven Attacks

Threat actors have utilized large language models (LLMs) in their attacks as long as the technology has been widely available. Early applications involved generating convincing phishing lures or conducting basic data reconnaissance, but recent evidence shows attackers deploying AI to execute end-to-end attacks, assist with malware development, and more. More recently, attackers have abused — and continue to abuse — agentic penetration testing tools to break into target environments at machine speed.

In this attack specifically, Symantec said it did not identify the initial access vector, focusing more on the timeline it was able to glean from its post-incident investigation. According to the blog post, the attacker worked at first by hand, which investigators determined due to artifacts like typing errors.

When every staged payload was terminated by security software, indicators suggest attacker tactics changed when they tried again the next day. "For almost two hours," Symantec said, "the attackers submitted long, error-free PowerShell scripts with labelled output sections and, in places, comments that read as a model's reasoning." Approximately 10 minutes after querying the victim's SolarWinds Orion monitoring software, attackers managed to laterally move to a second server.

The blog post hypothesizes that the attackers behind the attack were likely financially motivated, as they searched point-of-sale scripts for passwords, and one address they contacted was linked to an operation that stole card data from online retailers.

Related:Artex: The AI Pen-Test Tool Hackers Turned Into a Weapon

During the second-stage activity, the threat actor gained initial access to a Web server and stole credentials from configuration files tied to the SolarWinds Orion monitoring software. And while the idea of AI speeding up or improving attacker tradecraft is nothing new, the attack is its deployment of AI to a hands-on keyboard attack in progress and possibly seizing victory out of an apparent defeat. It presents LLMs as a difference-maker for a less skilled threat actor.

Dick O'Brien, principal intelligence analyst on the Symantec Threat Hunter Team, tells Dark Reading this incident is one of several the team has seen in recent weeks where AI revived an attack. While he calls this a game-changer for attackers, "defenders can potentially leverage that pattern" as AI behaves in a particular kind of way, such as testing variants of a technique in quick succession.

"The retry pattern is a signal itself," he says. "Blocking on behavior rather than file names or exact commands matters much more. Treating a blocked attempt followed by a variant as a high-priority alert is worth considering."

Although no vulnerability was exploited and no patching was required, O'Brien believes this trend of AI accelerating attacks is and will continue to affect the patching race. "Our view is that defenders need to start looking at mean time to mitigate rather than mean time to patch. Patching is still important, but it can’t be the only countermeasure."

Related:CISA Announces Enhanced Reporting Form for Cyber Incidents

At Dark Reading, he covers a variety of cybersecurity topics, including the cybercrime ecosystem, open source security, and the intersection between AI and threat actors.
