#9784. Welcome Beam: a 501B open model you can own, customize, and scale

Beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face! It is the first model from the new US lab, Reflection, and it’s open! It's a mixture-of-experts (MoEs) model with 501B parameters (23B active per token), supports text as input, has a context window of 1M tokens, and is released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases. It is for teams that want a frontier-scale model on their own hardware, infrastructure, or cloud, and want to customize it to their own use cases. Beam ships with its own dedicated open source Rust based harness that delivers the best performance from the model.

Beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang. We’ve worked with the Reflection team to bring you inference, SFT (supervised fine tuning), and RL (reinforcement learning) recipes for you to build with this model for your needs. On top of day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM, this post shows you how to run it, how to post-train it, and what we built with it.

Reflection is going to give out $10,000 Hub credits to the best projects that use Beam. All you have to do is make a thing, and share it on the Hub:

If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build the space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. We’ll collect all the links, select the best, and send out the credits to your Hub accounts.

Beam is a text-only model built for long-context (1M context length) reasoning and agentic work. It is a sparse MoE model, where each token is computed by a small fraction of the network, so it runs at the speed of a much smaller model while keeping the capacity of a large one.

The decoder has 52 layers with a hidden size of 5,120. Most layers use sliding-window attention over the previous 512 tokens; every sixth layer, and the last one, attend to the full context. That gives 43 sliding-window layers and 9 global ones.

Inside the attention block (both layer types)

The two kinds of layers handle position differently. Sliding-window layers use RoPE, since relative position matters most within a short window. Global layers use no positional encoding. Instead, each query is multiplied by a scaler that grows slowly with the number of visible tokens, (1 + (pos + 1) / 2048) ** 0.1. It acts as a temperature: the softmax keeps its precision as the context lengthens instead of flattening out. The implementation calls this scalable-softmax query scaling.

Attention uses grouped-query attention with 48 query heads and 8 key-value heads, with RMSNorm on queries and keys. A learned sigmoid gate, computed from the layer input, scales every channel of every head before the output projection.

The first 3 layers use a dense SwiGLU MLP. The other 49 replace it with a Mixture-of-Experts block of 256 experts, each a SwiGLU MLP with an intermediate size of 2,560, or about 39M parameters. The experts hold 98.4% of the model's parameters.

The router follows DeepSeek-V3's group-limited scheme. It scores all 256 experts with a sigmoid, splits them into 8 groups of 32, keeps the 4 best groups (ranked by the sum of each group's top two scores), then picks the top 8 experts inside them. Beam uses the same group sizes as DeepSeek-V3 but no shared expert. Expert outputs are combined with normalized router weights and scaled by 2.5.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 23B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of a 501B model but runs at the speed of a 23B one. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores most parameters in 4-bit precision for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, some parameters are kept in BF16 for accuracy. There are also FP8 checkpoints on the hub which are ideal for Hopper and Ampere series chips.

If you want to deploy Beam yourself, check out the vLLM or SGLang recipes below.

The residual connections are the most distinctive part. A standard transformer adds each sublayer output to the stream with weight 1, so the stream grows with depth.

Beam counts the input embedding as step 1. At step k it adds the sublayer output with weight 1/sqrt(k) and keeps the existing stream with weight sqrt((k-1)/k). The squares of the two weights sum to one, so the stream stays at a constant scale from the first layer to the last. After all 104 additions, every sublayer output and the input embedding carry the same weight in the final hidden state.

Every sublayer is also normalized before and after, and the final logits pass through a tanh softcap at ±30, computed in FP32. The implementation fixes where it computes in FP32: the router, the SwiGLU product, the norms, RoPE, the query scaling and the softcap.

Hybrid attention works well for long contexts. Each layer caches 2 x 8 KV heads x 128 dims = 2,048 values per token. If all 52 layers kept every token, the cache would grow by 208 KiB per token. Only the 9 global layers keep the whole sequence. The 43 sliding-window layers hold a fixed 512-token window each and stop growing. So the cache grows by 36 KiB per token, roughly a sixth of the naive rate.

These numbers are per sequence, in BF16, with the transformers dynamic cache.

Here are the benchmark results across different precision levels, as provided by the Reflection team.

The most practical way to serve the model is serving the NVFP4 checkpoint, which retains most of the quality of the bf16 checkpoint. NVFP4 stores some weights in 4 bits, and this way, it shrinks the 501B parameters in BF16 from 1 TB to ~280 GB. Blackwell GPUs run NVFP4 natively but GPUs older than Blackwell like the H200 can't. The FP8 checkpoints are suitable for GPUs older than Blackwell.

A B200 has 180 GB of HBM3e, so two of them (360 GB) can hold the Beam weights, with little room left for activations and the KV cache. Plan for four B200s (720 GB), which leaves plenty of room for long contexts and concurrent requests. You can also serve it on a full 8xB200 node, or on two B300s at 288 GB each, or even 8xRTX Pro 6000. If you don't have Blackwell hardware, use Inference Providers (serverless) to test Reflection.

Beam comes with day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM.

Install the latest version of transformers.

The easiest way to run Beam is the text-generation pipeline:

The pipeline returns the whole chat. The last message is Beam's reply, already parsed by the response template.

Going one level lower, use AutoModelForCausalLM and AutoTokenizer.

Beam's tokenizer carries a response template. parse_response reads it and turns the raw output into a message dict, with the reasoning, the answer, and any tool calls in separate fields. This avoids the usual regex for splitting reasoning from answers from tool calls. And the rules ship with the tokenizer, so the parsed structure matches what Beam was trained to produce. The chat template can pre-write part of the assistant turn, which the parser needs to see.

Pass tools to parse_response as well. Beam writes tool-call arguments inline, in its own XML-style grammar, so a bare 7 could be a number or a string. With the tool schemas, the parser casts each argument to its declared type.

Beam's config defines an expert-parallel plan. Expert parallelism puts each expert on one device. Attention, the dense layers, the embeddings and the LM head are replicated on every device. That is 8B parameters, or 16 GB in BF16. Load the model with a DistributedConfig:

Launch the script with torchrun across 16 H200 GPUs. Each one then holds 78 GB of weights. With 8 GPUs each would hold 139 GB, which leaves no room on a 141 GB H200. The number of devices must divide the number of experts, 256.

Beam has day-0 support in vLLM. The command below serves the BF16 checkpoint with tensor parallelism across 16 GPUs (two 8x H200 nodes) and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:

For faster generation, add DFlash2 speculative decoding. A small drafter model proposes up to 15 tokens ahead, and Beam checks them all in one forward pass, so each step can accept several tokens. The cost is a little extra memory for the drafter:

Both commands start an OpenAI-compatible server, so you can point any OpenAI client at http://localhost:8000/v1. For additional serving configurations, see the proposed Beam recipe for vLLM.

Beam also has day-0 support in SGLang. We recommend serving it with DFlash2 speculative decoding, which both commands below turn on. On Blackwell, the NVFP4 checkpoint fits on 4 B300s:

On Hopper GPUs, use the FP8 checkpoint on 8 H200s instead. Only three flags change: the checkpoint, the tensor-parallel size (8 instead of 4), and the attention backend (fa3 instead of trtllm_mha, which needs Blackwell):

Beam is available on Hugging Face Inference Providers, powered by Baseten, Fireworks, and Together, with more to follow soon.

We’ve set up a Beam recipe for you to one click deploy in Inference Endpoints from the catalog in FP8 or NVFP4, or install with the hf cli like so:

We are sharing some vibe evals of Reflection Beam-501B-A23B on five tasks, once each at low and high reasoning effort through the Reflection platform. These are vibe evals, not benchmarks. If you’re planning on using Beam, this is a great way to kick the tires and see how it behaves on specific use cases, and importantly, where it wins and loses.

Below is an overview of the prompts we ran and the output traces from the hub. The complete inputs, outputs, API usage, task fixtures, graders and conversation traces are in this public Hugging Face bucket.

* Low's long-context response got all code behavior and all six source citations correct. However, the response did not correspond to the parsers format, so this is partly prompt ambiguity.

† Low returned the correct answer, but omitted the requested justification. High supplied a correct roots-of-unity proof, independently reviewed.

Don’t take our word for it. Dig into the bucket, rewrite for your use case or project and push Beam to the limit.

You can fine tune Beam for your own use cases. Here, we share some examples in TRL and Miles to get you started on supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.

The quickest way to adapt Beam to your own data is supervised fine-tuning with TRL's SFTTrainer. To keep memory manageable, we train LoRA adapters with PEFT rather than updating all 501B parameters: We used TRL’s SFTTrainer to adapt Beam to a simple goal: keep its reasoning in the language requested by the user. We fine-tuned on Multilingual-Thinking with LoRA, which trains a small set of adapter weights while keeping the base model frozen.

The setup combines model sharding at load time, expert parallelism, FlashAttention 4 and sequence packing. LoRA SFT fits on a single node with 8 B300 GPUs, reaching around 19,000 tokens per second. The corresponding H100 setup uses four nodes.

After one epoch of Multilingual-Thinking, Beam reasoned in the requested language on 16 out of 16 held-out prompts, compared with 3 out of 16 for the base model. This small evaluation measures language adherence, rather than the correctness of the reasoning itself.

Training loss (left) and mean token accuracy (right) during a separate 500-step run on a reasoning subset of open-r1/Mixture-of-Thought, using one 8-GPU B300 node. These training metrics are from the official TRL example PR.

Reflection and RadixArk built a recipe that trains the model with GRPO in Miles, in BF16. You can update the full model or use LoRA to train adapters while keeping the base weights frozen. Megatron trains, SGLang generates the rollouts, and Miles publishes the new weights to the rollout engines after each update. We reviewed the recipe.

The recipe runs GRPO on DAPO-Math-17K and evaluates on AIME25. Build the image, download the data, and submit the job to a Ray cluster of twelve 8x H200 nodes:

Sample: 32 prompts are passed to the model with 8 responses each. Two SGLang engines serve the rollouts on 16 GPUs each.

Score: the boxed answer is checked against the label, with a soft penalty for responses near the length limit.

Update: one optimizer step on all 256 samples. Group-relative advantages with truncated importance sampling, no KL or entropy penalty.

Train in parallel: tensor parallelism 8, expert parallelism 8, data parallelism 8, with sequence parallelism and full recompute.

Optimizer: Adam at a constant 1e-6. Gradients in BF16, master weights in FP32, moments in BF16. The optimizer state streams through node-local NVMe, so each trainer node needs 2 TB of scratch.

Evaluate: AIME25 every five rollouts, eight samples per problem. A checkpoint is saved every twenty.

The next rollout is generated while the current one trains, so responses are one update behind. Add --resume to continue from the last checkpoint. execute-colocate runs the same recipe on eight nodes, with every GPU training and serving in turn.

You can also run GRPO with LoRA on four 8× H200 nodes: 16 GPUs for training and 16 for rollouts. The recipe trains rank-16 adapters on Beam’s attention, dense MLP, and expert layers while keeping the base weights frozen. Only adapter weights are synchronized with SGLang, and the optimizer state stays in GPU memory, removing the need for NVMe optimizer offloading.

If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build a space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. To inspire you, here are a few things we built.

At Hugging Face we love open and local models that run native to their hardware, but building native apps on Mac can be hard! Let’s see if Beam can help us out.

We asked Beam to build a native MacOS application that turns speech to text, and conveniently drops it at your cursor. We want to use MLX to get the most out of our Mac Metal and the Parakeet Model for great speech-to-text.

We used Beam with the Pi coding harness to build the initial native macOS menu bar app, running Parakeet with MLX. The saved run includes follow-up prompts; the final source also includes later Codex repairs. The prompt above is a condensed version of the build requirements.

You can check out the agent trace of how Beam built this in pi in this trace. If you want to try the demo out, download the source code or read the setup instructions.

We wanted to see whether Beam could make faster progress by splitting a programming task across agents. We paired Beam with the open-source Pi coding agent and compared three setups: 1. one agent working alone, 2. five persistent peers collaborating through a shared Git repository, and 3. a lead agent delegating work to asynchronous subagents. The harness ran on Hugging Face jobs with inference through Reflection’s platform API.

For the tasks, we used ProgramBench: agents must recreate a program from its compiled executable and documentation, without seeing its source code or the evaluator’s tests. Each setup had the same 8M API-token ceiling and two-hour solver limit per task, shared across its agents. We saved implementation snapshots and evaluated them against fixed hidden-test suites from the ProgramBench-Tests dataset.

Our score-versus-latency plot shows the average fraction of tests passed. The time axis uses fixed reference rates for model tokens plus measured tool time, rather than elapsed wall time. We initially ran five tasks. The current figure shows a post-hoc subset of jq, xsv, FIGlet, and hexyl; ripgrep was excluded across all three setups because grading its saved artifacts was too slow. The published results retain all 15 original episodes.

You can inspect the runs in the Trackio dashboard, explore the published result data, and reuse the study harness.

Decision models are all the rage at the moment because they’re super fast and practical for many use cases. We started with Beam in Pi after Beam’s quota ran out to train and evaluate a custom decision model for developer incident triage.

We wanted to see whether a coding agent could turn an incident-triage policy into a small, fast decision model. The task was to read a developer incident and choose the responsible team, its severity, and whether someone should be pinged immediately. Using Unsloth, we fine-tuned Qwen3.5-0.8B to score these choices directly.

First, the workflow built a synthetic dataset containing 2.3k incidents split by incident cluster for training, calibration, and testing. We trained a LoRA adapter and decision head for three epochs, with a 4-bit backbone, on one H100 80GB on the Science Slurm cluster.

For a baseline, we prompted the unadapted model with the full triage policy and ticket, without examples, and asked it to generate the three decisions as JSON. On the same 320 synthetic test tickets, the fine-tuned decision model got all three answers correct on 76.25%, versus 4.69% for prompted zero-shot. Mean ticket latency fell from 1,218.06 ms to 102.58 ms, an 11.9× speedup.

If you want to try out this experiment for yourself, check out the artifact bucket which contains the data, code, checkpoints and results.

Beam is a 501B open model that you can run on your own hardware and change. Start with the BF16 checkpoint, or try one of the quants FP8, NVFP4. If you build something with Beam, share it in the discussions tab.

Show interactive benchmark results with downloadable data

Well why don't you build something that can run on cunsumer GPU like Qwen 3.8 Flash Next for example using strata ?

That’s a good question. Apart from large corporations, no one would be able to set up this model in a way that allows it to function properly—it requires 8 RTX 6000 graphics cards, which would cost around 150,000 euros in total.

Thanks for sharing this! Small nit, but would you be able to add higher resolution diagrams for the model architecture figures? They come out pixelated for me (and possibly others) so I can't read the smaller annotations in the figures.

This is a genuinely exciting release — 501B Apache 2.0 with 1M context is the kind of thing that makes "open" in open-source mean something again. The residual stream design with the 1/sqrt(k) weighting is a nice touch; it's the sort of architectural detail that makes a real difference at scale without being a headline feature.

One question from the NLP side: the post focuses heavily on coding and agentic use cases, which makes sense for the target audience. But how does Beam handle multilingual text? I'm asking specifically because the 1M context window is exactly what you need for cross-lingual document understanding, and if the training data is skewed toward English + code, that's a gap that matters for non-English research communities.

Also — is the training data or at least the data mixture documented? For a model this size under Apache 2.0, reproducibility of the training setup is part of the open-source promise, and I'd love to see it.

In this episode, Christopher "CRob" Robinson, CTO of OpenSSF, Akrites and Chief Security Architect of the Linux Foundation, explores the state of software supply chain security amid multiple security incidents and explains how tools like Scorecard, the Security Baseline framework, and SLSA help harden software.

The article describes an architecture for agentic AI in regulated utility operations. Agents reason and propose actions, but a deterministic policy gate and a governed tool gateway control execution, with human approval where required. It covers an AWS reference implementation, grounding in runbooks, governed prediction, outcome validation, audit evidence, and phased autonomy.

Sundara Raman Ramachandran shares how LinkedIn productionizes LLM ranking under strict P99 latency SLAs. He discusses distilling a 7B model down to 400M parameters, compressing job contexts into single-token embeddings for a 10x throughput leap, and eliminating hidden system bottlenecks - from custom flash attention masks to Python GIL workarounds, gc.freeze, and non-blocking CUDA memory copies.

Henry Wilson shares actionable tools from the BBC Sounds re-architecture to help senior engineering leaders drive technical strategy. He discusses building buy-in, navigating active resistors, using RFCs and ADRs, and balancing tradeoffs - showing that effective software architecture is fundamentally about communication, relationship-building, and organizational influence.

InfoQ Homepage News Airbnb Introduces CASTLE for Training Natural Language Search Models with Synthetic Data

Nov 16, 2026 2 min read

Airbnb researchers have introduced CASTLE, a framework designed to address the cold-start problem in natural language search. The approach uses de-identified booking sessions and large language models (LLMs) to jointly generate synthetic search queries and relevance labels, enabling model training before sufficient real search traffic is available.

Natural language search allows guests to describe their preferences in everyday language, such as "romantic cabin near skiing" or "pet-friendly beach house that sleeps eight", rather than relying exclusively on predefined filters. Training such systems presents two challenges: generating queries that reflect actual user behavior and determining which property listings are relevant to each query.

Previous approaches, including InPars and Promptagator, address query generation and relevance labeling as separate tasks. They use LLMs to generate queries from documents or examples, followed by additional model-based judgments to assign relevance labels. According to the researchers, this separation can introduce additional sources of error and differences between synthetic and real-user query distributions.

CASTLE uses contrastive listing pairs derived from de-identified booking sessions. When a guest books a property after viewing several alternatives, the selected listing becomes a positive example, while another viewed but unbooked property serves as a negative example. An LLM is then prompted to generate a query that matches the positive listing but not the negative one. This allows relevance labels to be established through the construction process rather than through a separate evaluation step.

The framework combines three query-generation strategies: template-based prompts, few-shot prompts using approximately 500 seed queries collected through targeted user research, and attribute-grounded prompts focusing on distinguishing listing characteristics. A variety mechanism also encourages variation in query length and phrasing.

For listing pairs without sufficient booking history, including newly listed properties, CASTLE uses a Virtual Judge, an LLM-based evaluator that assigns relevance labels to additional query-listing pairs. The researchers also developed CASTLE-R, a variant intended for production environments where real search traffic has started to accumulate.

In the evaluation, CASTLE achieved a Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence of 1.01 against real-user query distributions, compared with 9.33 for the best baseline, Promptagator. This represents a 9.2-fold reduction in divergence. At the attribute-type level, CASTLE achieved a KL divergence of 0.08, compared with 0.09 for manually curated survey seed queries. Source: Medium Blog

The researchers also conducted a human evaluation in which three independent subject matter experts reviewed 200 sampled triplets. Agreement with CASTLE's relevance assignments ranged from 91% to 93% across the three evaluators.

The evaluation methodology also prompted discussion on LinkedIn. Mark Tsai, an AI Engineer specializing in LLM fine-tuning and evaluation, raised a question about potential overlap between training and evaluation data:

Do the training and evaluation splits keep seed templates and listing IDs disjoint? For synthetic triplets, I’d compare a random split with that stricter split, then evaluate on untouched real queries. It would help separate learning reusable intent–attribute matches from recognizing familiar templates or properties.

Wendy Ran Wei, the article's author, responded that the team evaluated the model on untouched real queries and implemented leakage guardrails when constructing evaluation sets. She also clarified that the paper does not report a controlled comparison between random splits and stricter splits with disjoint seed templates and listing IDs, identifying this as a possible direction for further investigation.

#9782. How Rust Changed Me As A Developer

The programming language you use affects how you think as a software developer 1. That may seem surprising to you; you may have picked up JavaScript pretty quickly knowing Python, and it didn't really affect how you think or develop. That's because those languages are pretty similar. The more different a programming language is from what you're used to, the more it can change you. Rust was quite different to me, so it did.

I've been developing with Rust for over 6 years; more than 4 years professionally now. One of the reasons I really wanted to become more proficient with Rust is because I knew it would challenge me, and hopefully change me for the better as a developer. I think it did.

What I learned and am going to discuss here is not exclusive to Rust. You can encounter many of these concepts in other contexts, and indeed I had encountered quite a few of them already. But in this case, Rust helped bring them into better focus.

We're all familiar with product types, though not usually under that name:

The fields of the Human struct 2 can vary independently from each other, and we have to deal with all possible combinations: all possible first names and last names, combined. The product of their combinations, to to speak.

But it turns out there's another type thing that's been around forever but that the programming community has mostly been been ignoring 3: the sum type. A sum type expresses variants: something is either one thing, or another, out of a bunch of variants:

A Person is either a human or a cat: that's the sum of the possiblities. Each variant can have data associated with it, and this can be a product type, but the Person type is just these options (two in this case). In code where you need to deal with a person, you need to handle each variant by match in on the object. The Rust compiler enforces this.

When you handle the human variant, you only need to worry about first_name and last_name. You don't have to worry about name or cuteness at all. These cases are distinct from each other.

It turns out that it's really helpful to model stuff using sum types. People using functional programming languages already knew this. You can model optionality (null) this way: you got either some value, or nothing. You can also model errors: it's either okay (with whatever value you return in case of success), or an error (with a value describing the error).

Any language without sum types now feels impoverished to me. I know I can simulate it with some type field, but the job of a programming language is to help me handle basic stuff, and this is basic stuff.

In an object oriented programming language, you handle variants using dynamic dispatch and an interface (or inheritance). You do this:

The idea is that you can now use Person anywhere without worrying about the details inside: it's loosely coupled. You only use their interface.

This is indeed a great idea, but Rust taught me that this has tradeoffs I may not want to pay for. You pay two things: performance, and the need to create the interface.

Let's talk about the need to create the interface. You need to devise an interface that actually makes sense for your application: how are you using humans and cats everywhere? Doing this work of abstraction may be extremely worthwhile to do, especially if you anticipate unknown future persons that you need to be able to plug in later without having to modify the code that uses them -- you want your code use the open/closed principle.

But what if you are developing a single domain, and inside that you just want to be able to handle cats and humans and that's it? There's just no need to plug in other types of persons, and certainly not from outside.

Or let's say you do want to add a new variant once every while. Say you want to add Dog. Maybe you're actually okay going through the code that handles Human and Cat and add handling for dogs too? Maybe it actually is helpful to see those other handlers right there too when you do so? The compiler is going to ensure you don't miss any spots!

Or what if the abstraction you are trying to devise is the variance and that's more or less what you can say about it? For error handling, the abstraction is either okay with some value, or some error value.

In this case you may be paying the price of creating an interface without it being worthwhile.

enum may be all you actually need -- low ceremony, and statically checked. Finally I'll note that enums don't lock you out from creating that abstraction - you can add methods to an enum too, just like on a struct.

Enums made me a better programmer as now I have another elementary, simple, easy to understand language construct for abstraction in my mental toolbox.

In many languages there are two types of dispatch: dynamic dispatch, which we've discussed in case of our Person interface, and conditional dispatch, like this:

Rust has dynamic dispatch, if you ask for it. It also has the powered up version of conditional dispatch I already discussed: match on enums. It has conditional dispatch too - that's just [a special case][https://docs.rs/bool/latest/bool/enum.Boolean.html].

There's another type of dispatch that Rust makes you think about: dispatch that's statically compiled.

What if you're dealing either with groups of humans or groups of cats, and you want to do some operations on them, and those operations have common behavior (say, you want to count them). The group, or collection, doesn't really care about what's in it, as long as every item fulfills certain basic properties.

You could create an enum Person; either an enum or an interface with multiple implementations, and then dispatch during runtime to every member of the group based on whether that entry is a human or a cat. But this means you have to account for mixed groups of humans and cats, even though we just said those don't actually exist.

Instead, you can express this differently in Rust. You still have a Person interface (trait), but you compose your individual type of Person (Human or Cat) during compile time.

Rust now refuses to compile if you use non-cat operations on items in the group, That's an invariant you now do not need to worry about anymore. This will be familiar to you with generics in other languages like TypeScript or Python.

In Rust, when you process your group of cats, there is no individual check somewhere whether an entry is a human or a cat, as it already knows it's all cats before the program even ran. Rust directly dispatches to the cat code, and the human code is not play. You avoid indirect dispatch for every group member, which can matter in situations where performance is important.

Rust made me a better programmer as I now better understand the connection between dispatch and performance.

When I discovered Python coming from C++ back in the late 1990s, dynamic typing was a revelation. You could so much with so little ceremony. For the last decade or so I have been on a long winding road back to types (far more ergonomic types) and more ceremony. I have the impression many have been on this journey along with me 4.

Types can statically check your code before it runs. In Rust, they can help the compiler compile stuff down to really high performance code. Both are great. But types can also have more subtle benefits. Let me get into this by analogy.

Obvious: Automated tests ensure various properties of your code work and remain working.

Subtle: Writing tests forces you to think about the architecture and APIs you're implementing more carefully. Making code testable can lead to better architecture. This is the insight of test driven development.

Obvious: People (and now machines) can understand 5 the why and what of your software by reading the documentation.

Subtle: The act of writing the documentation can force you think about the architecture and APIs of your software. If you can't write about it, maybe you haven't gotten it right yet? That's documentation driven development.

Obvious: Statically check your code before it runs! Prevent runtime errors! Performance!

Subtle: You model the domain model using types, trying to make sure it hangs together. Enums are really valuable here. You express parse, don't validate in them. The types guide the architecture and APIs of your software.

This perhaps sounds like big design up front processes where people write all the tests, or all the docs, or all the types, in advance, and then do the implementation. 6 I'm not talking about this -- I'm talking about iterative development where you keep going back to tests, docs and types as you learn.

Rust brought into focus how types are yet another tool to help me think while I develop.

Rust made me a better programmer as it let me fully embrace type driven development.

Here is the biggest surprise I had coming to Rust. Much of the behavior I associated with dynamic interpreted languages with a rich runtime like Python can actually be done statically in Rust using macros.

Say you want to dump the state of a Python object -- you inspect all its fields, look at their type, turn each into a string, combine all the strings together into a big one. Now you can store it somewhere. Later on you restore that string back into an object. You can save and load any objects: magic! Python calls this pickle.

What if you need to serialize to JSON? Python has a type system, and a library like Pydantic inspects the type objects during runtime and then uses this information to let you automatically serialize a Python object to JSON, or parse it back into Python again. More magic!

Rust is a compiled language. Types aren't runtime objects. Without reflection, which takes special effort, runtime introspection of types is not a thing in Rust.

But Rust can still do what Pickle and Pydantic do, at compile time.

With serde, Rust's answer to pickle and Pydantic, you use a normal Rust type, annotate it with a few declarations, and then you can serialize it to JSON, or toml config format, and many other formats, and load it back again. The annotation looks like this:

With clap, you create the type that expresses exactly what command line arguments you expect (with enums too!), document it using the normal way you document any API in Rust, and boom, you have a CLI with built in help. The code that handles the various cases gets well-typed data - at that point it's been parsed correctly already, using the same type you used to express the CLI.

Again declarative #[] stuff going on. It looks a lot like decorators in Python. But Python decorators are executed during runtime, and we just said Rust doesn't normally let you do that.

How does that work in Rust? Macros! Macros lets you write code that generates code during compile time. With serde, the macro generates a whole bunch of serialization code and deserialization code for the types annotated with it. This generated code gets compiled along with the rest of your code. The compiler can optimize it just like any other code.

Code generation is scary. Macros are scary. Doing introspection in a dynamically typed language is a lot easier than using Rust macros, where code is parsed and generated. Macros shouldn't be randomly mixed with application code; macros belong in frameworks. That said, something being easy doesn't mean it should be used casually: in Python you typically want to carefully encapsulate your magic in a declarative framework too.

Rust made me a better programmer as I learned about a new class of framework patterns.

Rust famously lets you write code without memory leaks that doesn't use a garbage collector. It also stops you from mutating data you're also reading elsewhere, making it impossible to stumble into whole classes of weird undefined behavior, especially with code that runs in parallel.

Rust's ownership system is one of the main things that makes learning Rust hard. Python, JavaScript, Java and many other languages have mutable references everywhere, and you can just create cyclic data structures. Rust won't let you do either out of the box.

The equivalent of this does not compile in Rust:

Rust won't just let you have circular references, in this case both children and a parent reference.

This feels very limiting at first! What do you do instead? For mutating stuff, you learn how to separate mutation (often during construction) from using your data. That is a thing that's good to do in many contexts -- less invariants makes it's easier to reason about, but it takes a bit of getting used to Rust strictly enforcing it.

For circular references it's trickier. I will go into it next, when I discuss arenas.

A weird thing happens: if you lean into this friction it can improve the architecture of your codebase. Code becomes less coupled. It's hard to create weird backchannels with action at a distance that makes code difficult to understand, test and debug 7.

Rust code locally can be difficult to understand. But how the data flows, what does what, in the larger codebase, tends to be cleaner.

Rust made me a better programmer as I now think about ownership more carefully, which has a positive impact on architecture.

A few years ago I analyzed a bunch of XML tree libraries in Rust. The best I found, roxmltrree, has an immutable tree. But I needed a mutable tree. I found quite a few libraries that did support mutability, but many did not support parent references. You couldn't walk up the ancestor chain of a node. This, along with missing support for some XML features, is why I created my own in the form of Xot.

The reason for this surprising lack of parent references is the ownership limitation I discussed before: Rust makes circular references difficult. You can get around it using reference counted types and internal mutability, but in a lot of cases this pattern isn't really optimal -- it's verbose, less performant, and reference count cycles risk memory leaks. What you do instead is store nodes in an array and you use the array indexes to node as your reference. You can then have an index referencing your parent, and use index references to your children, or any other circular reference.

A fancy word for this pattern is an 'arena' and in Rust they show up everywhere.

In an arena, you store a lot of objects together in the same region of memory (in an array). What does it let you do?

iterate fast over its contents. Objects being in the same memory region means the CPU can use its cache effectively. This is much faster than arbitrary main memory access and loops really benefit.

fast allocation. The arena is allocated from the heap as a block, and after that your allocations may just be a few increments.

interning: you store something once in the arena and use it in many places, so you don't duplicate data.

the arena owns its stuff. Everything in the arena has the same lifetime. Indexes between objects in an arena can be circular without worrying.

Rust pushes you to use arenas. This involves more ceremony than just using a direct reference, but it also means Rust pushes you to write code that computers can execute really efficiently.

I mentioned performance a number of times. But what about premature optimization? The great irony of this quote is that it comes from a paper where the author, Knuth, argues in favor of keeping the goto statement around, as it's essential for writing efficient software.

Rust lets you know what you pay for. Reference counting? Dynamic dispatch? You can do it, but it's going to be visible in your code. Rust also often lets you know when you don't want to pay for it: just look at tower middleware and despair about all the generic types and type constraints that get piled onto a relatively simple abstraction.

When you have these tools available, need to develop new wisdom about tradeoffs that never seemed to matter. If you write Python code you're not too worried about hash tables being a performance bottle neck, but in Rust code they certainly can be. You can get lost along the way into hyper optimization land. Often you need to just get go 8. Many patterns that are just plain readable Rust code anyway happen to also be friendly to the CPU executing it.

But Rust overwhelming you with details you may not want to think about is not the whole story, because performance is not just quantitative: if your code can truly be more performance, it can access new qualities. When you can write code that uses no memory and no CPU time 9, it changes how you think. It changes what's possible.

Sometimes the quality of performance is obvious: if you write numerical code, or a simulation, of course you don't want to wait for the answer. Being able to do many computations really fast is key to making AI possible.

But it's more subtle that that: modern computers are really powerful, and ridicously fast, and we generally ignore that and just throw more resources at our problems. There are good reasons why this happens. But if we open our eyes a little, there are new architectural possibilities we can explore.

While the power of macros were the biggest language surprise, I think this is the biggest shift in my thinking: access to performance unlocks possibilities I hadn't considered before. Take my experiment Colchis: a library can store vast amounts of JSON in memory, while retaining full access, even indexed access (I still hope to add jsonpath one day!), to JSON data. Before Rust, this was a possibility that wasn't even on my radar.

Rust made me a better programmer because I can make the computer do more with less, opening up new areas of opportunity.

Rust is one of the most difficult programming languages I've learned -- and thus one of the languages that changed me the most. There's a simple part of Rust that isn't much harder to manage than any language, and in some cases may actually make your life easier -- enums, declarative type-driven frameworks, and the excellent dev tooling come to mind. Even arenas are fundamentally not that difficult to understand. The complexity is in unlearning some habits and learning new ones. And then there's a more challenging complex Rust, mostly, but not always under the surface, there when you need it.

Rust expands the reach of what I can build. That's what makes me happy I went on this journey. 10

AI agents write a lot of code. They know the programming language, so do you need to know it? Does the language still affect the developer? If you share my belief it's good to look at the code, then it helps if you understand the code you're reading. I also think it's never been more important to think about how the systems you use affect the way you think and behave.

If you don't know what a struct is, just call it a class in your head, and you're good.

You have them in many languages but in impoverished forms, like true/false, or C's enum.

If you're going to do static type checking anyway for the guarantees it brings, perhaps use a language designed around it (enums!) that also gives you performance benefits?

Does AI truly understand? Do you want to have a philosophical debate? What do we mean by understand? Natural language is inherently stretchable.

With AI we've seen the return of big design up front. I may be wrong, but I'm still skeptical of this approach, and still a fan of iterative development and incremental learning and theory building.

Not impossible. I've seen it. People can do it if they really try, and it still makes life harder; it makes it much harder to test. But at least it's more obvious and more difficult to do.

Clone and own all the stuff! Which incidentally can also lead to more contiguous memory layouts...

No memory and no CPU time is an exaggeration, but little Rust programs sometimes feel that way.

AI development is shifting all the tradeoffs in software development - they're not gone, but they have shifted. The AI can write Rust, even if you don't know it. But I trust plenty of contexts remain where my Rust experience plus AI leads to a better outcome than AI by itself.

#9780. TorchNeuron: running HF models on AWS Trainium is easier than ever

TorchNeuron provides a new native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels natively support it, making it easier than ever to run models on Trainium and to share them on the HF hub.

TorchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a new backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP. Read the Pytorch blog to learn more about TorchNeuron.

Starting Oct. 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta. Researchers and developers will be able to install it with pip install torch-neuronx.

To date, the Hugging Face experience on AWS Trainium and Inferentia — AI chips designed respectively for cost-effective training and inference at scale — has been delivered through optimum-neuron. This library relies on the torch-neuronx package, which is based on PyTorch XLA. It was the natural choice at the time, but it meant thinking like a compiler: lazy tensors instead of eager execution, static shapes only, a recompilation for every graph break. Optimum Neuron existed to hide that complexity, and maintained custom code (modeling classes, trainers, etc) to do so.

TorchNeuron changes this. It integrates directly into PyTorch and exposes neuron as a native device, with eager execution, PyTorch's own distributed primitives (DTensor, FSDP2) and torch.compile.

For the Hugging Face libraries, Trainium becomes a device like any other: Transformers, Diffusers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL run on it directly, with the same classes and scripts you would use on any other accelerator. From now on, we recommend that Neuron users use these libraries directly instead of going through Optimum Neuron.

Text generation is now natively supported in Transformers for a wide range of models. With TorchNeuron, 89% of the top 100 most-used text-generation model architectures are supported out of the box, compared to 46% with Optimum Neuron v0.4.5. You just need to pass the device_map=neuron argument in your code and your model will be moved to the Neuron devices.

The following is an example of text-generation with tensor parallelism, which will enable to fully benefit from your Neuron instance. Note that it uses a static cache for generation as this is strongly recommended with Neuron to prevent frequent recompilations.

Now that Neuron is a native PyTorch device, training on Trainium uses the same Hugging Face libraries as any other accelerator: Transformers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL. You no longer need a dedicated trainer or a Neuron-specific fork of the model code. A standard TRL fine-tuning script runs on a Trainium instance with only a few Neuron-specific settings.

Here is a supervised fine-tuning script built on TRL's SFTTrainer. If you have fine-tuned a model with TRL on GPUs before, it should look familiar.

Parallelism is handled natively by Transformers. You put a DistributedConfig with the tensor-parallel (TP) and FSDP sizes in model_init_kwargs, SFTTrainer passes it to from_pretrained, and the model is sharded as its weights are loaded. The Trainer sees that the model is already distributed and does not wrap it again. You don't need an --fsdp flag or an Accelerate FSDP config.

Nothing in the script is tied to Trainium: the same code runs on any hardware. A few things are worth knowing when you run it on Trainium:

The command below launches training with torchrun, which starts one process per NeuronCore. TP_SIZE and FSDP_SIZE set the parallelism layout, and their product is the number of processes: here 4 x 8 = 32, matching --nproc_per_node. The 32 processes form a 4 x 8 grid. Tensor parallelism splits each layer across the 4 cores of a TP group, and FSDP shards the parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the 8 TP groups.

We ran it on 8 Trainium2 chips (32 NeuronCores), which is half a trn2.48xlarge instance.

Training runs to completion, and trainer.save_model writes a standard Transformers checkpoint. Nothing in it is tied to Neuron: you can push it to the Hugging Face Hub as is and load it on any other hardware.

Many pipelines from the Diffusers library are compatible with TorchNeuron in eager and compiled mode. FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.2, Qwen-Image, Qwen-Image-2.1 and H3 are also compatible with tensor parallelism to make the most of your Neuron devices. The following is an example showing how you can use TP:

You can run this piece of code with: NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=2 torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 run.py.

More and more pipleines will be compatible with TP. If a pipeline you like is not, you can also add support for it following this guide.

Make sure to check out the kernels from the Neuron team as more and more Neuron kernels will become available on the Hub to speed up your models. Neuron kernels can be written using the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI), which gives lower control to optimize operations. This way, users can run their own custom operations and share them on the hub.

You can use for example this kernel to speed up your vision transformers with up to a x2.4 speedup on Trainium!

Special thanks to the AWS team for their work on TorchNeuron and for their reactivity to our feedback to make the HF integration as good as possible.

hi, which models are supported with this? is mobernbert and t5gemma2 on the list?

Hi, we now have a space where you can chek if a model is supported: https://huggingface.co/spaces/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support

InfoQ Homepage News Uber’s Legal AI Agent Cuts Contract Review Time by 20% with Rules and RAG

Nov 16, 2026 2 min read

Uber’s Legal Redlining Agent has reduced average contract review time by more than 20%, with 91% accuracy in AI-generated decisions, according to the company. Integrated into Microsoft Word, the agent analyzes proposed contract changes, assesses legal risks, and recommends policy-aligned responses using retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), historical lawyer feedback, and deterministic rules. Lawyers retain responsibility for reviewing and approving its recommendations.

The agent identifies edits proposed by external parties, interprets their intent, compares changes with legal policies, and suggests whether to accept, reject, or modify clauses. It also generates comments explaining recommendations and flags changes requiring closer scrutiny. Uber began developing the first generation in early 2024 and piloted it with its Legal team in 2025.

High-level workflow of the Legal Redlining Add-in / Agent (Source: Uber Blog Post)

An initial RAG implementation retrieved relevant sections from legal playbooks to guide language model responses. However, the system struggled with semantic retrieval accuracy, negotiation tone, and scenarios not covered by existing examples. Uber subsequently added a feedback loop that captures lawyers’ decisions, reasoning, and final edited text.

This change allowed the agent to retrieve examples of how similar clauses had been handled rather than relying only on whether a previous recommendation was accepted or rejected. At runtime, similarity search and metadata filtering narrow thousands of historical interactions to approximately 20 candidates. A second language model-based filtering stage evaluates their relevance. Exponential decay weighting, with a configurable half-life currently set to 365 days, prioritizes recent decisions while retaining older examples. The implementation also gives domain experts control over language and negotiation style.

Uber Engineering framed the challenge in its LinkedIn post:

How can AI help streamline repetitive contract review while keeping lawyers in control?

The legal team defines the desired tone and style, while engineers maintain the prompt structure and application workflow. The architecture combines a React and TypeScript Word add-in with a Python backend orchestrated through LangGraph. Parallel workflow nodes handle intent detection, risk assessment, and policy lookup. OpenSearch stores vectorized legal rules and historical feedback, while Redis maintains session state for follow-up questions.

Legal Redlining Agent system architecture (Source: Uber Blog Post)

A deterministic rules engine enforces non-negotiable legal requirements and overrides model recommendations when a matching rule applies. Language models handle tasks requiring contextual interpretation, including clause recommendations and negotiation tone. A final verification step checks generated responses against retrieved rules.

Uber is also exploring agentic harnesses, including Claude Code and OpenCode, alongside skills to structure and automate workflows across its agentic AI efforts. The team plans to investigate legal ontologies and knowledge graphs to represent legal concepts and relationships, providing a semantic foundation for more consistent interpretation and reasoning.

#9777. MPS in PyTorch 2.15

If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and new Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.

A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.

If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:

You'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why.

To try the release candidate in a separate environment:

FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.

You can multiply these tensors with F.scaled_mm, which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:

Every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each new token goes through the model as a single row, so the big matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.

MPS has had GEMV kernels for torch.mm since 2.14, but F.linear still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to F.linear, so the common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.

A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation.

In 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The new Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well.

For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:

The decoding kernel shows up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with torch.compile, MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second:

Working with complex tensors gets easier. complex64 LU factorization, LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:

Small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: QR uses blocked updates, and triangular solves turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.

Gated DeltaNet workloads get a dedicated fast path for batches of 16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems with at least eight right-hand sides.

SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles very small singular values, very large or very small input magnitudes and basis completion with full_matrices=True, which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.

Audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them new paths through Metal:

Token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. softmax and log_softmax now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a [1, 128256] row of logits drops from 57 µs to 7 µs, about 8× faster than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes:

One of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers makes 8,764 padding calls over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about 270 GiB to 8 GiB:

You can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. torch.mps.Stream and the torch.mps.stream context manager provide the interface, and Tensor.record_stream lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream.

Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result:

Several more operations now run on MPS: torch.frexp, torch.logspace, torch.take and Tensor.put_, torch.heaviside, torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l and unsigned-integer comparisons. logspace doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element.

Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now handles batch and head broadcasting correctly.

Work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on main and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.

Once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 commits the command buffer every 16 kernels, so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:

Scaled dot-product attention is dropping MPSGraph completely: every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms.

The move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm forward and backward are in progress, while MSE loss (up to 12× faster on small inputs), std_mean and var_mean (up to 4× faster) and bincount have already landed. bincount is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond.

Bundled shaders will build for Metal 3.1 by default, with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks libtorch_cpu.dylib by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication.

PyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try!

A big thank you to Nikita Shulga, Kurt Mohler and Aaron Gokaslan for reviewing much of this work, and to everyone who contributed to MPS in this release.

#9776. [$] Zellij manages terminal workspaces with style

Zellij is a relatively new entrant in the terminal-multiplexer category. Like GNU Screen and tmux it gives users the ability to manage a workspace inside a terminal with split panes, provides session management, and so forth; but Zellij also includes a web server for browser access to a terminal session, is extensible via a plugin API, and is likely more beginner-friendly than its predecessors. Its most recent release, version 0.46, adds a standalone terminal emulator, a built-in inbox for notifications, and a settings screen so users can configure the application without fussing with configuration files. While the low version number might suggest that it is not yet ready for serious use, it seems stable and full-featured enough to meet the needs of many users.

#9775. AnyLanguageModel 1.0: One Year of Local Models on Apple Platforms

Last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback.

Local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this new generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task.

A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0.

The core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement:

The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below.

Over the past year, we've added several major features:

On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models.

Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps.

Support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports:

With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too big to run on the device with the same session code:

Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses.

Reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the new provider can't replay them.

API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy.

AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server.

While we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now:

The first two fit on an iPhone, and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more. Selecting the MLX model takes one line:

And if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16. For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers.

If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel, swift-huggingface, and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code.

Community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers.

Language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device. Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen.

InfoQ Homepage News Java News Roundup: Lazy Constants, Spring for Apache Pulsar, GlassFish, Hibernate, TomEE, Seed4J

Nov 16, 2026 5 min read

This week's Java roundup for November 9th, 2026, features news highlighting: Lazy Constants proposed to target for JDK 28; TornadoVM jitLLM 3.0; point releases of Seed4J; second release candidates of Spring AI and Spring Boot; first release candidates of Hibernate ORM and Hibernate Reactive; fourth milestone release of GlassFish; and the second milestone release of Apache TomEE.

JEP 547, Lazy Constants (Fourth Preview), has been elevated from Candidate to Proposed to Target for JDK 28. This JEP proposes a fourth preview, with no changes, after three rounds of preview delivered in the upcoming release of JDK 27 and JDK 26 through JDK 25. Formerly known as Stable Values and Computed Constants, this feature introduces the concept of computed constants, defined as immutable value holders that are initialized at most once. This offers the performance and safety benefits of final fields, while offering greater flexibility as to the timing of initialization. The name change from Stable Values to Lazy Constants with the release of JDK 26, better captures the intent of a high-level use case. The review is expected to conclude on Wednesday, November 18, 2026.

Build 24 of the JDK 28 early-access builds was made available this past week featuring updates from Build 23 that include fixes for various issues. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

For JDK 28, developers are encouraged to report bugs via the Java Bug Database.

The second release candidate of Spring AI 2.1.0 delivers new features such as: a new DecisionModel API, anchored by the DecisionModel interface, that returns the probability of different outcomes instead of generated text based on yes/no answers, questions about text or a set of fields; and a new similaritySearch(float [], SearchRequest) method, added to the VectorStoreRetriever interface to complement the corresponding overloaded methods, to search with a user's embeddings in more vector stores. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.

The second release candidate of Spring Boot 4.2.0 ships with bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: support for reading the value defined in a X-Forwarded-Prefix HTTP header in a WebFlux application on Reactor Netty when the server.forward-headers-strategy property is set to native; and a database assigned to the spring.data.redis.database property is now properly applied to master/replica connections if a value is assigned to the spring.data.redis.masterreplica.nodes property. More details on this release may be found in the release notes and this wiki page.

The Spring for Apache Pulsar team has announced that the project is moving as a subproject within Apache Pulsar at the Apache Software Foundation to "foster even deeper integration and collaboration with the broader Pulsar community." As stated in the blog post:

Bringing this integration directly into the Apache Pulsar project allows the community to streamline development, accelerate feature support, and ensure long-term alignment with the evolution of Apache Pulsar.

Spring for Apache Pulsar 2.0.8, released in October 2026, was the final release under the auspices of the Spring ecosystem.

The fourth milestone release of GlassFish 9.0.0 provides bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: implementation of the Jakarta Persistence 4.0.0-M7 specification with EclipseLink 6.0.0-M1; a move of the Sun Theme module out of the out of the external GlassFish Woodstock Components repository into its own module in GlassFish so that Sun Theme and the Admin Console can be modified together; and an update to versions 1.2.0-M2 and 2.0.0-M1 of Eclipse JNoSQL. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.

Beehive Lab, makers of TornadoVM, has released version 3.0 of jitLLM, a JVM-native LLM inference and serving engine, delivers notable changes such as: 1.43 times faster startup with GraalVM Native Image; an up to 9.3 times faster prefill phase; and a more efficient reading of model weights by eliminating the copy from the mapped GGUF file into a Apple Metal buffer. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

The first release candidate of Hibernate ORM 8.0.0 ships with notable changes such as: an implementation of the Jakarta Persistence 4.0.0-M7 and Jakarta Data 1.1.0-M4 specifications (the latter via Hibernate Data Repositories); and support for coordination of graph-based flushing that builds a dependency graph for pending entity and collection mutations. Further details on this release may be found in the what's new page.

The first release candidates of Hibernate Reactive 5.1.0 and 5.0.0 provide notable changes such as: the EXTENDED constant, defined in the Jakarta Persistence PessimisticLockScope enum class, now locks the collection tables as intended to align with the same functionality in Hibernate ORM; and an update to the VertxFactory interface to allow for adding observability without changing the functionality in using the DefaultVertxInstance class. These versions are compatible with Hibernate ORM 8.0.0.CR1. More details on these releases may be found in the release notes for version 5.1.0.CR1 and version 5.0.0.CR1.

The second milestone release of Apache TomEE 11.0.0 delivers bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: resolutions to 38 CVEs; completion of their implementation of the Jakarta Authorization 3.0 specification; and TomEE Plume, the enterprise version, now ships the modular EclipseLink JPA artifact instead of the eclipselink Uber-Jar. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.

The release of JobRunr 9.0.4 ships with bug fixes and one new feature that improves build caching and security by moving to hardened Docker images. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

The first rolling release of JReleaser 2.0.0-SNAPSHOT provides a new feature in which the -a and -d short option flags, for their respective corresponding --assembly and --download long versions, were removed from the CLI due to the lack of short option flags for the --changelog and --announce flags. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.

Versions 2.4.0 and 2.3.0 of Seed4J, formerly known as JHipster Lite, deliver bug fixes, dependency upgrades and new features such as: install Playwrite only on applications that execute the relevant Playwright component tests; and improved efficiency by creating one global Maven cache that is shared by the Seed4J build and every generated Maven application that replaces a Maven cache for each generated application. More details on these releases may be found in the release notes for version 2.4.0 and version 2.3.0.

The Quarkus team has introduced the Quarkus Resiliency Testing utility that allows developers to reproduce various failure scenarios and their respective responses while testing an application with the @QuarkusTest annotation. An example application using this new utility may be found here.

Presented by: David Iparraguirre - Senior Product Marketing Manager at Datadog, and Jessica Yang - Product Manager at Datadog
